With regard to the report of the departmental committee which had under consideration the character, quality and suitability of the

boots supplied to the first Canadian contingent, laid on the table of the House to-day, I think it desirable and in the public interest, and also due to the various manufacturers who supplied the boots, that the report of the committee and all matters which it concerns should be referred to a special committee of the House, in order that the subject may be further investigated, if desirable, and that the committee may report to the House in due course its findings with regard to the whole matter. Accordingly, I shall move to-morrow, when motions are called, that a committee of seven members be appointed for that purpose. If my right hon. friend will give me to-day the names of three hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, I shall be glad to have their names included in the list of members of the committee.

A report appeared in the public press to-day to the effect that aeroplanes coming from the United States had been sighted. Can the right hon. Prime Minister give me any information on this point?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am afraid that I am unable to give the point of departure of the aeroplanes in question. The only information I have on the subject is that about nine o'clock last evening the mayor of Brockville telephoned to me that three aeroplanes had crossed over Brockville, going to the north, and that one of them had turned a searchlight upon the town, lighting up very considerably the principal street. On receiving the information I communicated it to the chief of the general staff, with the suggestion that it should also be made known to the Commissioner of Dominion Police.

On the Orders of the Day being called:
Mr. 0. TURGEON:	(Gloucester, N.B.):
I rise to a question of privilege. My attention has been called to an article in the St. John Standard of the 11th instant, in which certain assertions of mine are misrepresented. I am reported as having used the following words at a recruiting -meeting:
I <lo not see how Britain can expect the men of Gloucester county to volunteer or enlist to light her battles when they are obliged to leave their homes and go to the United States to earn their living and a living for their families.
I brand that report as an infamous distortion of fact and language. Others may call it what they wish, but that is what I think of it. I believe that no member of this House-especially you, Mr. Speaker, who have heard practically all my utterances in this Parliament during the last fifteen years-would say that I would use these remarks before the people of Gloucester county. I believe too that the diatribes contained in that report are not the views of the editor who wrote it. It has been published, no doubt for a purpose, one month after I made the declaration in Tracadie; but every man from New Brunswick knows that I was the first to organize and call recruiting meetings in Gloucester coupty and along the north shore of New Brunswick, as is shown by the correspondence with the Canadian Patriotic Committee of St. John, New Brunswick, of which His Honour the Lieutenant Governor of New Brunswick is president and Mr. Jas. Gilchrist is secretary. At my instance, eloquent speakers have attended these meetings. One of them in Bathurst was addressed by a gentleman whose name is familiar throughout New Brunswick, more particularly to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, Mr. F. M. Sproule, a member of
the legal profession, an ex-member of the legislature, one of the most eloquent speakers it has ever been my pleasure to listen to, and the next morning fifteen or seventeen young men from Bathurst enlisted before dinner. If I had allowed this statement to go without contradiction some one, not in this House or in New Brunswick, might have believed it. I did not wait until war was declared to pronounce my allegiance or my loyalty to the Crown. My allegiance was my birthright and my loyalty has grown stronger with each year of my life. At the last meeting I addressed I did say, at the end of my remarks, after calling on the young men to enlist, that the young men of the county of Gloucester had not responded as generously as I had expected, although more generously than those of any of the surrounding counties. The number was not to my satisfaction. I said that, owing to the hard times prevailing in Gloucester since the year before, owing to the depression of business, such as the closing of the iron mine at Bathurst by which three or four hundred men were thrown out of employment, many of whom had gone to the United States and were therefore not here to enlist, a larger number should have gone to the front. I shall not take up your time by reading the diatribe against me that follows, as I have said I do not think that the editor of the Standard himself believes it. If any further explanation is required at any time I shall be glad to give it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BORROWINGS BY CANADIAN BANKS FROM THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The Government does not regard it as expedient to give detailed information as to the advances made to individual banks. This policy follows the precedent established in 1907, when loans were made through the Bank of Montreal and details were not only not giv*n as to loans to banks but are not even of record in the Department of Finance. I do not make this statement by way of criticism, because I think it was sound policy. There is another reason which I am sure will appeal to my hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte) why detailed information should not be given. In 10i
the letter which I addressed to the several chartered banks on September 5. 1914, giving notice of the proclamation which was issued by the Government under the authority of the Finance Act passed at the special war session in August, I stated:
All applications to the Treasury Board will be regarded as confidential, and it is my earnest hope that we shall have the hearty co-operation of the banks in bringing into effect the new legislation.
Under all the circumstances it would seem to me that my hon. friend might possibly be disposed to refrain from pressing his application for particulars.

subtopic: BORROWINGS BY CANADIAN BANKS FROM THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: At this moment I express no opinion as to whether or not the information should be given to the House; I simply call the attention of the Minister of Finance to -the precedent of 1907, when, if my memory serves me, the advances were made either to the Bank of Montreal itself or upon guarantee of the Bank of Montreal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BORROWINGS BY CANADIAN BANKS FROM THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
My right hon. friend is correct in this, that the Bank of Montreal made and guaranteed the advances, but that does not at all alter the fact that advances were made to banks from Dominion funds. There was the additional security of the guarantee of the Bank of Montreal, but there is no distinction in principle. If it is advisable to make public details of loans made to the banks upon any security, it would appear to me that the same principle would apply, although the security is enhanced by a guarantee of a bank, even though that bank may be an institution such as the Bank of Montreal. The principle is the same: Advances were made in Dominion notes upon security.
There is the further consideration, not necessary for me to emphasize unduly, that last September it was very desirable in the public interest that the banks should be made to feel quite free to avail themselves of this legislation which had a two-fold object, namely, first, to conserve the gold supply of Canada, and, secondly, to enable the banks the better to supply the commercial needs of the community. In those circumstances, I wrote the banks pointing out that such was the object of the legislation; and in order that they might be more readily induced to avail themselves of its provisions, I stated, as I have already mentioned to the House, that their applications would be regarded as confidential. Under those circumstances, I think it would be a violation of the understanding between them

and the Government that we should bring down details. As a matter of fact, the total amount advanced the banks has been comparatively small, as shown by the answer to the question of the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte), and a substantial part has already been repaid.

Montreal, January 27, 1915.
Sir,-In accordance with the Order in Council dated January 5, 1915, authorizing me to examine the foundations of the Victoria Memorial Museum at Ottawa and report thereon, I beg to make a preliminary report as follows:
In order to deal intelligently with this matter there are points that should be definitely established, viz:
(1)	To what extent has settlement occurred in the foundations of the building.
(2)	Has such settlement affected the stability of the building.
(3)	Is this settlement still going on.
When these points have been determined, and if it is found that settlement is still going on, it would then be in order to point out what steps should be taken to prevent further settlement in the future.
After an examination of the building, I will consider this subject under two heads, namely:
(1)	The foundations of the main building.
(2)	Foundations of the tower and heavy cross wal\s.
Main Building.
With regard to the settlement of the foundations of the main building there can be no question. How much this has amounted to is, however, more difficult to determine. There seem to be no plans in existence which show the original elevations of the footings or piers, nor have any observations been made to determine the progress of the settlement. The amount of settlement, however, can be arrived at approximately by comparing the present elevations of footings which have been subjected to unit loads of varying amounts. On the outside walls of the building an estimate of the weights shows that there is approximately an average pressure on all the bearing areas of about three tons per square foot. On the interior sub-basement walls and footings of columns there are loads varying from one to two tons per square foot. The result is that the outside walls have gone down much faster than these interior walls or footings.
This movement is more plainly in evidence on the ground floor, which is supported at the centre, on two rows of columns resting on light interior walls in the sub-basement, and at the sides on the main walls.
Accompanying this report is a blue print dated January 27, 1915, showing elevations which I have had taken on this main floor. The cross sections and profiles shown thereon indicate at a glance what the settlement amounts to at all points on this floor.
The settlement around the four walls of the east and west wings is shown to be fairly uniform, although there seems to be about one inch more settlement towards the north face of these wings. From the cross sections of these wings it would seem that there has been between 5 and 6 inches settlement of these walls, assuming that there has been little or no settlement of the interior walls.
There is nothing to show that the interior walls in the two wings have settled to any appreciable extent. While the average elevation of the floor over these walls is about one inch higher in the west wing than in the east wing, yet it is quite possible that some of this difference may have occurred in the original laying of the floor.
The interior walls of the main building do not show such a regular line, the settlement being much more pronounced near the main tower and wings. This, however. can be accounted for from the fact that these walls, being incorporated in the heavier walls of the tower and cross walls, would be carried down simultaneously with the latter.
From the elevations taken it wTould appear that settlement of the walls of the main building amounts to from 5 to 9 inches. The slope of these walls is. towards the main tower, where the greatest settlement has taken place.
This indication of the settlement of the main walls is practically confined to the ground floor and basement. On the first, second and third floors, where the supporting girders extend from wall, there is little or no evidence that any such settlement has taken place.
As regards the stability of the walls of the main building, I do not consider that this has been seriously affected. If the ground floor had

been supported on long girders extending from wall to wall, similar to the floors above, there would be little or no evidence to show that settlement had taken place, except of course at points where it is incorporated with the walls of the tower and the heavy cross walls. Cracks have opened up in the walls of the east and west entrance, which would naturally be expected, but this result could not in any case prove serious, A few of the stone lintels and ,mullions of the building have been cracked but not to any serious extent. The greatest evidence of this settlement is shown in the basement, which is sub-divided into offices with light brick partitions. These partitions rest on foundations having a very much smaller load to the square foot of area. The result is that when the outside wall settled its tendency was to shear past these lighter walls or to carry that portion of the wall nearest the main wall down with the latter, thus opening up cracks in the brickwork. These partition walls are only one story high. and. outside of the unsightly nature of the cracks, their displacement has no bearing on the stability of the bu!lding. From a thorough examination of the basement I find that the relative action between these walls is practically uniform.
The question as to whether settlement of the foundations of the main building is still going on is one that at present I am not prepared to answer. While it is an undoubted fact that considerable settlement has taken place, it may be possible that the soil has become compacted to such an extent that further settlement has stopped. On the outside of the building there is nothing that would point to the fact that settlement had taken place for a considerable length of time. At the rear of the building there is a concrete sidewalk which was laid hard up against the base course of the walls, which sidewalk, I have been informed, was constructed three years ago. If settlement had taken place in that time I would look for some evidence of cracking or distorting where this sidewalk joined the building. It is possible that the ground under th s sidewalk may be more or less loose and that the walls, if settling, would carry the sidewalk with them. In this case, however, I would look for a tilting or cracking of this walk, which does not appear. While this point is not conclusive evidence, yet to my mind it is sufficient to raise serious doubts as to whether settlement is taking place at the present time.
In the basement, where the partition walls between the offices join the main walls, there seems to be a certain amount of evidence that a movement is still going on. Several occupants of these offices have informed me that cracks in the brick veneer of the main wall and in the partition wall have been opening up within the last eighteen months, and in one or two cases there seems to be evidence that the cracks have increased in length during the past few months. In other offices, cracks which had been puttied up two or three years ago, have opened very slightly. As the brick veneer on the main walls, has an air space of one inch or so behind it and is not cemented directly on the main wall, it may be that there is some local action taking place between the partition walls and this brick veneering which may be entirely independent of any pr sent action of the main walls. It would appear, how-

ever, from the consensus of reports, that the movement during the last eighteen months has been very slight. In view of the evidence obtainable, it would seem that the only way to determine whether any action is really taking place on the main walls of the building would be to have. ** series of accurate readings made on the outside cf these main walls, sue' [DOT]'endings to extend over a sufficient length of time to enable an intelligent and definite report to be made. I have taken steps to have such a series of level readings taken, and have given instructions that checks on these points be taken at regular intervals in order that this information may be obtained.
Main Tower and Cross Walls.
The settlement of the main tower and cross walls is considerably more pronounced than that of the main building. This is undoubtedly due to the fact that the load on the footings is very much higher. On the main tower the average pressure on all the foundations of the piers and walls amounts to about four tons per square foot. On the cross walls the load per square foot varies from three to four tons. As in the case of the main building, it is also difficult to determine exactly what the total amount of settlement has oeen. While the tower has gone down a certain amount as a ?vhole, it has, however, gone down much faster at the front wall, the rear wall being undoubtedly supported to a certain extent by the other walls intersecting thereat. At the present time the tower has an inclination from the vertical of about twenty-four inches, measuring from the highest point of the tower to the loot of the foundation. This means that the ex-tieme outer edge of the foundation is 10 J inches lower than where it joins the main walls of the building.
There is no doubt in my mind but that the displacement of this tower is sufficient to cause anxiety for its ultimate safety. In moving forward it is taking the main walls of the building with it. The result has been to open up serious cracks in a portion of this wall and cause serious doubts as to its stability. So great has been the movement of this tower that the steel beams of the 4th floor, which were resting on this tower, have, I am told, pulled entirely out and have had to be supported on special girders. The cracks in the walls between the cross walls of the main building and the tower have been opening up continually and have been filled up from time to time as they became apparent. It is, moreover, quite apparent that movement is still taking place. Last September, I believe, all openings at this point were plastered up, but at the present time this crack has opened up again about l inch, and at one point daylight can be seen through the wall.
An indication that the tower is still settling is shown by the sidewalk at the front entrance. Last September, I understand, a new sidewalk was laid at this point with a grade sloping away from the building. At the present time this sidewalk has an inclination in the opposite direction, or towards the building, and where it joins the building, is several inches lower than at points in the near vicinity. I would judge from the nature of the soil and the loads that have been distributed upon it that there is every possibility that settlement will continue to go on until the stability of the tower is seriously menaced. This menace is magnified

from the fact that as the tower continues to lean outward the centre of gravity also moves outward, increasing the pressure on the extreme toe of the foundation and thus tending to increase the rate of movement.
The cause of the trouble wThich has arisen in connection with this building is due entirely to the fact that the soil upon which the building was erected has had loads placed upon it entirely out of proportion to its supporting values. This soil is a type of blue clay which, under ordinary conditions, should be able to support from two to three tons per square foot. The bearing value of clay as a foundation, however, is uncertain and great difficulty is very often experienced in foundations on this class of material.
On the interior columns, which support a load of about one ton per square foot, there has probably been little or no settlement, although I cannot verify this fact. On the outside walls of the main building there is an average of three tons per square foot. This has proved too heavy a load for this material as the walls have gone down from 5 to 9 inches in the last seven years. The loads under the tower have averaged 4 tons per square foot, the settlement at this point being considerably greater than under the walls of the main building. It is quite evident, therefore, that the first point tc be determined is the bearing value of the soil upon which the building rests. I have taken steps to this end, and a series of loading tests on the soil in the basement of the building is now going on.
Recommendation.
I would recommend that nothing be done with regard to the walls of the main building until a series of observations have been taken over a sufficient length of time to enable me to determine whether further settlement is actually taking place.
With regard to the main tower, I consider steps should be taken at the earliest possible moment to prevent further settlement. This can only be done by increasing the bearing area under this portion of the building. This is entirely an engineering problem, and in a later report I will advise what, in my opinion, is the best means by which this work can be successfully carried out.
I would say that I do not consider there is any immediate danger to the building, or that ir will be necessary to close it to the Government employees or the general public so long as the present rate of settlement is not in-ci eased. I have made arrangements with the chief architect to have a series of readings taken at the point where danger might be expected, so that any increase in this movement would be immediately noted.
T think, however, in view of the foregoing that the necessary steps should be taken by your department to have repairs instituted in connection with the main tower and effected during the coming summer.
Respectfully submitted,
(sgd.) C. N. Monsarrat,
Hon. Robert Rogers,
Minister of Public Works,
Ottawa, Ont.

speechtext:
Mr. F. B. CARVELL (Carleton, N.B.), moved:
For a copy of all correspondence, letters, telegrams, by any and all persons whomsoever, had with the Department of Railways and Canals, or F. P. Gutelins, General Manager of the Intercolonial Railway, or any other official thereof, with reference to freight rates over that portion of the Transcontinental Railway, province of New Brunswick, and also with reference to the removal of the Y connection at Wabski, county of Victoria, between the said Transcontinental Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway at that point.
He said: I wish to call the attention of the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane) to a matter of very great importance to the business community of the western portion of New Brunswick. And in doing so, perhaps the better w'ay, in order to make it plain, is to refer to a matter which is somewhat personal. But I hope the minister will understand that this personal reference is only to illustrate

what is really a public matter; nor is it purely personal, as it refers to my connection with an estate and what affects me in that capacity affects many other business men in that portion of New Brunswick. The House is aware, of course, that the Transcontinental runs in a diagonal direction from the northwestern corner of New Brunswick to the southeastern corner. In its course it crosses the Canadian Pacific railway at a place called Wabski, near Plaster Rock. It crosses the Canadian Pacific railway at an elevation of from one hundred to one hundred and fifty feet. When the Transcontinental was under construction, a branch line of about a mile in length was made and a connection was in this way made with the Canadian Pacific railway. This branch line was constructed, paid for, owned and operated by the Transcontinental down to three or four months ago, when the connection was destroyed and the rails taken up, so that there is no possibility of getting communication between the two roads. About a year and a half or two years ago I had occasion to bring this matter of railway rates and connections to the attention of the minister, and I complained that the Government was not taking any means, or was not taking the proper means, to promote business and industry in that portion of the province of New Brunswick. I pointed out that the rates charged on the Transcontinental were so exorbitant as to be practically prohibitive. I dealt with this matter in this House on the 21st of March, 1913. The minister, I think very much to his credit, was greatly surprised at the statement I was making, so much so indeed that he challenged the truth of it and wanted me to give a case in which the Transcontinental practically refuse^} to do business or undertook to do it only at rates so high as to be practically prohibitive. I at once called his attention to a statement of facts. He will find the debate in " Hansard '' of that year, pages 6816 to 6818 inclusive. Of this I desire to read now only one paragraph:
I happen to be the executor of an estate and during the past three or four months I have hauled by team between three and four million feet of lumber a distance of fifteen miles over probably the most hilly road in New Brunswick, to the Canadian Pacific railway. I could have hauled that very same lumber to the Transcontinental railway, a distance of less than five miles, and practically all down grade, between the mill and the railway. The party whom I represented was alive at the time the negotiations started in November, he died in December and since then, as the executor of the estate, I have been carrying on the business.

I went on to explain that we had hauled over 3,000,000 feet of lumber by team fifteen miles over a hilly road, and shipped it by the Canadian Pacific railway, because we could make more money than by hauling it five miles and shipping it by the Transcontinental. I will give the minister the credit of saying that he took up the case 4 p.m. energetically. He told me both publicly and privately that he would see justice done. The Transcontinental wanted 6 cents per cwt. to transport that lumber thirty-one or thirty-two miles, which means almost $1 a thousand feet on ordinary spruce lumber. That was prohibitive. He told me he would send Mr. Gutelius to me and have the matter arranged. While Mr. Gutelius did not come to me, yet, after considerable negotiation, an arrangement was made under which we were to get the lumber hauled at 4 cents per cwt., which would be practically $1.20 per thousand feet. That means that I was wrong in my first calculation-G cents per cwt. would be not $1 but $1.50 on ordinary spruce lumber. But I should think that $1.20 ought to be enough to satisfy even Mr. Gutelius, who, I presume, is animated solely by a desire to make money for the Government railway system. But, while the rate was exorbitant, still, in order to carry on business, we accepted it. In 1913 we did about the same amount of business, and got some money out of it, I am glad to say. We carried on the same business in 1914, and again made money. We had hoped to continue carrying on this business and still make money, but, early in the summer-I have forgotten exactly what date; I would give the minister the precise facts but that I have not the papers before me-the manager of the company was informed by the officials of the road that they would not accept any more freight at Wabski, that they were going to take up the connections, and that we would have to send our freight north on the Transcontinental to Theriault, which is practically fifty miles north of the connection at Wabski. There we should hand it over to the Canadian Pacific railway, who would have to bring it back on a line practically parallel to the Transcontinental and carry it to Boston. Fortunately for us, the Canadian Pacific railway charged the same rate from Theriault as from Wabski. If they had hauled the freight for the extra fifty miles for the same money we should have had no complaint to make. But it made a wonderful difference to other people. The man who had freight originating on the Canadian Pacific railway and wanted it
delivered on points on the Transcontinental, found the rate was prohibitive. But the Transcontinental, or Intercolonial railway authorities, not only wanted to haul the freight the fifty miles further, but wanted us to pay 7 cents per cwt. for hauling it, or 3 cents per cwt. in addition to what we were already paying. As the average of spruce lumber will weigh 3,000 lb. per thousand feet, this extra rate would amount to 90 cents per thousand. This meant practical prohibition. After negotiation, they offered to carry the lumber at li cents per cwt. additional, which would mean about 45 cents or 50 cents per thousand, which, in many cases, is a large proportion of the profit a man makes on lumbering operations in New Brunswick. I was told at that time that the difficulty lay with the Canadian Pacific railway, who were unwilling to accept freight at the Wabski junction. I took the matter up with Mr. Bamford, divisional freight agent of the Canadian Pacific railway, at St. John, to whom I wrote on the 3rd of October, 1914. This correspondence is brief, and I should like to read it so that the minister may have the facts before him:
I fear very much that the minister knows only one side of this case; otherwise he would never have been a consenting party to the business outrage committed upon the people of that portion of New Brunswick. I admit that the words " business outrage " are pretty strong, but I know of no other words in the English language which would correctly describe tlhe transaction.
On October 3, I addressed the following letter to Mr. Bamford:
Dear Sir,-As one of the executors of the estate of Michael Welch, of Bristol, who in his life-time carried on a milling operation at Fores-ton. Dp to last year the lumber was hauled to your road at Bristol, but as the mill is within seven miles of the Transcontinental, we hauled it to Juniper and handed it over to your road at Wabski.
We have now nearly three millions of lumber to send to the American market during the coming winter, and would commence loading this just as soon as the snow comes, provided conditions were satisfactory.
Last year we obtained a 17 cent rate from Juniper to Boston. I do not know how it would divide up, but I always understood the Intercolonial railway got the lion's share.
Not long ago we were informed that your company objected to taking this lumber at Wabski, and therefore, it could not be handed to you until it reached Theriault, some distance below Edmundston, and we were told the rate would be 20 cents. We absolutely refused to do any business at that rate and decided that we would be compelled to haul to Bristol, and close down the business. Gutelius then came down to 18J cents, but still persists in saying

that your company objeeed to taking it over at Wabski, and therefore it must be taken to Theriault. This means about 50 cents a thousand, which eats up a.large portion of our profits, and if this condition of affairs continues, I see nothing to do but to close up the business.
Will you kindly write me and let me know just why this course is being pursued? If you are willing to take it at Wabski at the old rate, I will endeavour to give the matter such publicity that Mr. Gutelius will hand it over at that point. If, on the other hand, it is a mutual arrangement, probably the force would be so great, that the only move would be to shut down.
On October 19 I received from Mr. Bam-ford the following letter, which, in my judgment, was very satisfactory:
P. B. Carvell, K.C.,
Woodstock, N.B.
Dear Sir,-With further reference to your letter of October 3 in regard to lumber shipments from Juniper to Boston.
At Wabski the interchange of traffic has been permitted between the National Transcontinental railway and Canadian Pacific railway. A connection was put in at the time of the construction of the National Transcontinental railway to permit the contractors to get in their construction material. The connecting track was of considerable length and down grade. It is claimed by the Intercolonial railway that the steep grade rendered its operation very hazardous and difficult, particularly during the winter months, and that their train operating between Moncton and Edmundston was being badly delayed on account of the time taken to do the switching.
You mention in your letter that you were informed that the Canadian Pacific railway objected to taking this lumber at Wabski. This is not correct. Our rates are still in effect from that point to Boston, and on July 30, Mr. Grout wrote the Intercolonial railway to know if he would not continue the practice as it seems to him to be a very fair arrangement. To this he received a reply dated August 10. An extract read as follows:
' It has been decided that we will not transfer any more traffic at Wabski of any kind after the 15th Inst.'
In connection with this matter, I might mention that we have a published rate of 13 cents per 100 pounds at the present time from Theriault to Boston.
Trusting this explanation will be satisfactory.
Yours truly,	.
W. B. Bamford, Division Freight Agent.
In this letter Mr. Bamford puts the matter up to the Minister of Railways direct.. Without any doubt the blame comes back to the Minister of Railways-I am speaking now of the minister not in his personal but in his official capacity-for depriving the people of tlhat portion of New Brunswick of that railway connection to which as a matter of business justice they are entitled. I have given an illustration showing that the taking up of that connection and the denying to

the people of the right to do business means a matter of 50 cents on every thousand feet of lumber handled by one firm, with which I am connected purely in the capacity of an executor.
I do not know whether my reply to Mr. Bamford's letter is of any importance to the minister; if he wishes to see it I shall be only too glad to send the file over to him. I told Mr. Bamford that I was very glad indeed to learn that he was willing to carry out the arrangement; that I was then writing to the Minister of Railways and that 1 hoped to be able to succeed in having the old conditions re-established. I wish to read Mr. Bamford's reply, because it shows beyond the shadow of a doubt that the Canadian Pacific railway were not only willing but anxious to have this rate continued and to have this trade handed over to them at Wabski, and at no other point. Nevertheless, every business man in that part of the country was led to believe-I do not say by Mr. Gutelius personally, but certainly by the officials of the Intercolonial railway-that the Canadian Pacific railway were not willing to carry out this arrangement, and that it was in consequence of the protest of the Canadian Pacific railway that this connection was tom up and the people subjected to the extra cost. This is Mr. Bamford's letter, dated November 14, 1914:
Dear Sir,-I have your letter of the 4th inst., in reference to . the transfer of freight at Wabski.
We are perfectly willing to continue the interchange at Wabski, if the National Transcontinental railway will give us the business at that point. In the mean time, until I hear from you again I will not do anything further.
For your private information, we would prefer to have this traffic handed to us at Wabski, and so would a large number of saw mill men doing business in that district. We are in a better position to supply empty cars to handle the traffic than our competitors, having direct connection with the Maine Central, and as you are aware, they hand over to us from fifty to one hundred empty cars daily, and we will he glad to hand over a good share of them at Wabski.
I will he very glad if you will advise me the result of your negotiations with the Minister
of Railways, and oblige,
Yours truly.
I may explain that in reading over this letter a few days ago, I observed in it the word " private." I at once wired Mr. Bamford to inquire if I had his permission to use the letter, and received a reply giving me full permission to make any use of it that I wished to make.
After I had definitely ascertained beyond any doubt that the Canadian Pacific railway

were not only willing but anxious to accept trade at that point, I took the matter up with Mr. Gutelius, and here is a letter which I wrote him on November 4, 1914:
Dear Sir,-Some time ago I was informed by Mr. Welch, one of my co-executors of the Michael Welch estate, that you had refused to transfer any more freight at Wabski to the Canadian Pacific railway, and informed him that in future this freight must all go to Theriault, a point 50 miles further north, for which you wanted 3 cents additional. We promptly refused to have anything more to do with the road, when he was then notified that the rate would be reduced to li cents additional, or 6J cents in all, the net result of which means that we lose 50 cents a thousand on our lumber, and you haul it 50 miles and get the 50 cents. You possibly get out of it alive, we lose it absolutely. Mr. Welch was informed by your people that the Canadian Pacific railway refused to handle this freight at Wabski. I took the matter up with Mr. Bamford at St. John, and by his letter of October the 19th, he assures me that as early as July the 30th, Mr. Grout asked you to continue the practice as then established, to which you replied under date of August the 10th, as follows :
1 It has been decided that we will not transfer any more frame at Wabski of any kind after the 15th inst.'
This puts it up to your road without any question whatever.
I thought after appealing to the minister in the spring of 1913, that I had this matter settled once and for all.
Do you consider it a fair proposition that men along the line who would like to do business with you, shall be compelled to fight for the 5 0 cents which you get, which practically means their profits, when to the ordinary observer there is no necessity whatever for so doing? The Canadian Pacific are perfectly willing to accept this lumber at Wabski, and are also willing to give us a rate at Bristol with the view of transportation by team from the mill to that point. We have on hand now over two million and one-half of long lumber and over one million and one-half of laths, to be transported just as soon as the snow comes, and we would like to know whether you will still give us the rate in existence last year, or whether we will be compelled to haul this lumber 15 miles over the hills to Bristol, as will certainly be the case under present conditions. Hilda conduct may look like good railroading from your standpoint, but it is certainly death to the operator, along the line who is trying to do an honest business.
I am very anxious indeed to hear from you at your earliest convenience.
I have also been applied to by the Fraser Company, Limited, and others along the line who would like to continue doing business at Wabski, but will be prohibited should this unfair and unprecedented discrimination be continued. I would assume that you would like to continue doing business and until I hear from you to the contrary, am going to continue in that assumption.

speechtext:
In Madawaska county. The distance from Juniper to Plaster Rock, now Wabski, is thirty-two miles, and from Plaster Rock to Theriault, fifty-one miles, so it is fifty-one miles from the crossing of the Tobique to Theriault. I have taken the mileage from the Intercolonial folder.
I have here a lot of letters with which I shall not encumber the record; there are letters from the Fraser Lumber Company and others protesting against this interruption of traffic, and asking me, as a member from New Brunswick, to do what I could in order to have this injustice remedied and I promised them, of course, that I would do what I could. As you will see, two or three months prior to these things I had been trying to do what I could, you may say. from a personal business point, but at least doing all I could to have the injustice remedied. I waited some time but got no answer to my letter of the 4th of November to Mr. Gutelius. I waited two weeks and it was a surprise to me that I had to wait that time in a matter of such business importance without the courtesy of an answer. So I was compelled to write to the minister direct, which I did on the 16th of November, as follows:
My Dear Sir:
I am enclosing you herewith a copy of a letter, dated the 4th inst., which I addressed to Mr. Gutelius, General Manager, Intercolonial railway, Moncton, to which I received no answer, and as the letter is complete in itself, it is unnecessary to repeat the statements therein contained.
I cannot tell you how sorry I am that Mr. Gutelius has broken up the arrangement which was made over a year ago, after a persistent and somewhat public attempt on my part to have things straightened out.
You will remember after discussing' this matter in Parliament, you promised me that Mr. Gutelius would come here and arrange matters satisfactorily. While he did not come, yet he put the rate at a point where we could do business, and live, but even than 4 cents a hundred for 30 miles in carload lots, is exorbitant. Now to add on another one and one-half cents means prohibition. I simply put the matter up to you, and ask you to see that justice is done.
It is now 12 days since this letter was written, and as it is so late in the season something must be done immediately if we are to continue doing business, and I trust I will be more successful in obtaining an answer from you, than I have been from Mr. Gutelius.
I wish to say, to the credit of the minister, that I was successful in getting a let-

ter back the day he received my letter in Ottawa and, more than that, I got an answer from Mr. Gutelius two days later, so that no blame can be attached to the minister for any discourtesy -so far as replying to my letter was concerned-but I am sorry to say that was the end of it. I received a second reply from the minister dated 18th of November and also one from Mr. Gutelius dated the 20th of November. I shall read the letter from Mr. Gutelius in order that the railway side of the case may be placed upon " Hansard " as well as the business man's side:
Dear Sir:
Re your letter November 4th.
The transfer between the National Transcontinental and Canadian Pacific railway at Wabski was closed for the reasons as described by our Agent as follows:
'The distance from our main line to the Canadian Pacific railway track is about three quarters of a mile and two per cent grade practically all the way. We handle all cars both to and from their line and do all the switching.
'Should there ever be a failure of equipment such as the breaking of a coupling and taking a string of loads down the hill the damage would amount to more than the gross traffic for several months.'
This connecting track was constructed by the Transcontinental people to enable them to get material and contractors supplies up to the Transcontinental grade from the Canadian Pacific railway. It was not contemplated that it would be a point of transfer and as such it carries with it hazards to life and property that cannot be safely undertaken.
General Traffic Manager Hayes advises me that the rate from Juniper to Wabski which you desire to perpetuate was 4 cents per 100 lbs. He also advised that an offer has been made to your people to haul your lumber from Juniper to Fredericton for 4| cents per 100 lbs. and explains that if the Canadian Pacific railway will give you the same rates from Fredericton to Boston points as they give from Wabski or Theriault that the aggregate increase which you would have to pay is a half a cent per 100 lbs. and further if the Canadian Pacific railway would give you the benefit of the reduced haul it would make the rate from Fredericton a half a cent lower than from Theriault which is about one hundred miles shorter and that your Boston rate would he the same as via Wabski and the effects of the entire operation would he to give you minimum rates and give the railways an opportunity to handle by minimum mileage at minimum risk.
From the above explanation you will understand I trust that the sole object in not making this temporary branch line a regular transfer point is based entirely upon safety of operation and that our offer to haul to Fredericton at the low rate relieves the proposition of any charge of discrimination on our part.
Yours truly,
F. P. Gutelius.
You will see that he puts the whole thing on the agent, just as if an agent at a small country station had anything to do with the tearing up of the connection between two railways, a matter so important that if it occurred on private railroads we would have an order from the Railway Commission within twenty-four hours.
I want to discuss this matter with the minister from two standpoints, first from the standpoint of the company which I represent, for it is a material matter to us, and then from the standpoint of the general public. First from our standpoint, look at the absolute inconsistency of the minister's general manager of the National Transcontinental railway. He refuses' to haul freight thirty-two miles for four cents, but is willing to haul it seventy-one miles for four and a half cents. Just think of a business man putting up a business proposition like that. He is willing to haul seventy-one miles to Fredericton for four and a half cents and not willing to haul thirty-two miles to Juniper for four cents and the only objection to the Juniper line is that it has a down grade of two per cent. Millions of dollars of business is done all over Canada and the "United States on short railways with, not two per cent, but three per cent ard four per cent grades. My hon. friend knows that the Canadian Pacific railway crosses the Rockies in many places with more than two per cent grades, and then they talk of the danger of failure of equipment and the danger of a string of loads going down the hill and being dumped. There is danger of that occurring in any railway operation if it is not run properly, and we are not going to assume thatjthe Transcontinental or the Intercolonial will handle business so negligently that they will allow loads to go down hill because there happens to be a two per cent grade on the hill. It seems to me it is the most childlike defence to any reasonable proposition I have ever seen advanced by a business man in my experience. Then he goes on to say: If the Canadian Pacific railway will do what they ought to do. Well, unfortunately, this Parliament has not very much control over the Canadian Pacific railway, not nearly as much as I would like, but this Parliament and this Government have absolute control over the other two roads, and no matter how unfair the Canadian Pacific railway may be, this Parliament is the body that has the power to say what the Intercolonial

speechtext: What is it from Wabski?

speechtext:
Thirteen cents. Mr. Gut-elius agrees to have that freight for Fredericton for 4J cents but you add 14 cents and you get 18i cents, exactly the rate Mr. Gut-elius wants us to pay if he takes it round by Wabski. I do not care whether he takes it around by Quebec or any other place so long as he gets it to Boston and gets it to Boston at 17 cents a hundred. We would be satisfied but that does not satisfy the public. The Walsh estate is only one member of the public. He says that if the Canadian Pacific railway would reduce the rate and give us the benefit of the proportional mileage, although he does not suggest what it is, we would get a less rate, but unfortunately we have no power to compel the Canadian Pacific railway to reduce their rate from Fredericton to Boston and give us the proportional mileage. That is where the matter stands to-day. I do not care whether you haul by way of Theriault or by way of Fredericton-we pay fifty cents a thousand more than we paid last year. The Transcontinental railway haul this freight 32 miles and get 4 cents per 100 lb. for doing it. If they take it to Theriault they haul it 50 miles further and get 41 cents a hundred pounds for it, or they haul it a distance of 71 miles and get 41 cents for hauling it. It may be good railway business on the part of the Government to haul freight 50 miles for half a cent per 100 lb. but I cannot understand it. If they can make money by hauling that freight an extra fifty miles for half a cent they must be coining money when they get four cents for hauling it 32 miles. That may be quite plain to a railway man but I only try to size up things as they appear to an ordinary lawyer upon reading the rates, and I must confess that I do not understand it. Possibly my hon. friend, being a railway expert, will be willing to explain this most remarkable discrepancy as it appears to a lawyer.
Now, having discussed this matter from the point of view of the Walsh estate I desire to look at it from the standpoint of the public. If the Walsh estate were the only ones doing business over that line of railway it would only be a matter of their losing 50 cts. per thousand, closing up their mill and going out of business. But the Walsh estate is only a small proportion of the public which would like to use that road. I have protests from a very large number of mill owners. There is Donald Fraser & Co., who have the largest lumber mills in eastern Canada, a firm which are handling over a hundred million feet of lumber a year and a firm that handles probably-

speechtext:
The difference is so
little that it never would be considered for a moment with respect to the question of the rate; the rate would be the same. I would be very much surprised if there would be 25 miles difference between the two railways. But that is not the point. No matter what has been done in the past, and no matter what my hon. friend may argue as to what should be done in the future, the fact remains that my hon. friend has put himself out of the race. He is not in a position to compete, because he has torn up the connection by which he could compete. When this track was torn up, the Frasers had half a million feet of hard-wood piled at that Y connection. They were using the Y connection for a piling ground. I know what I am talking about, because I was there and saw it. I am familiar with the location, and they had the lumber piled there. I do not know exactly what they have done about it, but I know that they had the lumber and that they had erected a large piling ground out on this Y connection about a mile away to the southward in order to get it away from the danger of fire and to get it where it could be piled.
In shipping to a distant point like Boston, it makes a great difference in the weight of lumber, and consequently a great difference in the rate, as to whether the lumber is dry or not. I have also a protest from Upham, who runs a business eight or ten miles below Plaster Rock, on the Canadian Pacific railway it is true, but who has done some business by shipping from the Canadian Pacific railway over to the Transcontinental, and I have also a protest from J. B. McLaughlin & Company. This means that every man engaged in the lumber and other business in that portion of New Brunswick has only one line of railway at his disposal, whereas he might have two com-

peting lines to carry his produce to the market. How the Minister of Railways sanctions a policy of this kind is something that I cannot understand. After this letter was written I wired to Mr. Gutelius, stating that we wanted to ship to Boston, and that if he would give us a seventeen-cent rate to Boston via Fredericton we would ship it that way, hut I got no answer to that telegram. We have been perfectly fair from a business standpoint; we have done everything we possibly could, and we only appeal to the minister when we cannot get an answer from the general manager of the railway to a, reasonable business proposition. All we have got from the minister up to the present time is courtesy, and I admit we have had that. The tracks have been taken up, the connection is gone, and we are sending our lumber to Boston at a loss of fifty cents a thousand. A large part of the lumber we intended should go to Boston is going to St. John over the Transcontinental, and therefore, so far as that is concerned, I do not think we are losing any money by it, but we know this is only a temporary condition of things. We are sending lumber to England to-day which we could hardly give away there a'year ago, and that applies not so much to quality as to specifications. Until a year ago we could only sell deals 3 x 7, 3 x 9, and 3 x 11, whereas to-day they will take almost any specification and pay a good price. However, when the war is over, that condition of things will cease, and then we will have to pay this extra fifty cents per thousand or stop doing business. How the minister can be a party to carrying on that unfair transaction, I cannot understand. I could understand it if this road were being operated by the Grand Trunk Pacific, because the Grand Trunk Pacific could maxe connections with the Grand Trunk at Levis or Richmond Junction, and they might get down to Portland and Boston in that way, but the Intercolonial Railway cannot do that. What the minister says is, that he will haul this lumber fifty miles further to Theriault and fifty miles further south to Fredericton, and hand it over to the Canadian Pacific railway and make the shippers pay for it. I hope the minister will be able to make plain what to me is particularly dense at the present moment. I wrote to Mr. Gutelius on the 25th of November and I protested as strongly as I could against the injustice, point-114
ing out to him that we were losing fifty cents per thousand, and I have received no answer and no redress of the grievance. What is true of the Walsh estate is true of many other business firms who do business, in that portion of New Brunswick and it:, applies to other business besides the lumber-business. Probably for all time to come the great industry in the central portion of New Brunswick will be the lumber industry. While there are some parts of that region which might be made profitable as arable land, I believe that the greater portion ol central New Brunswick will always continue _ to be more productive and more profitable as a forest area than as an agricultural area. The lumber operators in that portion of New Brunswick have to import hay, oats, fodder, and everything which goes to carrying on their business. The only way the man who lives on the Tobique or St. John river can possibly get in his supplies is by the Transcontinental railway, taking the freight up to Wabski on the Canadian Pacific railway, handing it to the Transcontinental at that point, and distributing it thence. Florenceville is possibly the great distributing centre for farm produce in New Brunswick and Florenceville is only fifty miles from Plaster Rock. The next fifty miles east of Plaster Rock is the great lumbering centre of New Brunswick, so that the farmer who has produce to sell in that portion of Carleton county and that portion of the province to the north, can best distrib ite his produce from that point. As it is today, the merchant of Florenceville who sells hay or grain must send it to Fredericton, eighty-five miles distant, thence to McGivney's, the junction of the Intercolonial railway and Transcontinental railway, another thirty odd miles, or in all twice the distance it should be sent, and that extra haul the farmer or the merchant has to pay.

I am pointing out to the minister the real facts in regard to the business of our country; I am giving nothing fanciful, nothing got up for political purposes, because there is no politics in this matter so far as I am concerned. This is business, something that affects not only the lumberman but the farmer, the merchant, the business man everywhere. It is an injustice which the minister would never have allowed had he been seized of all the facts. I have endeavoured to place the facts before the minister from an entirely unprejudiced standpoint. I have read all the correspondence between myself and Mr. Gutelius. I have given my side of the case and Mr. Gutelius' side as well, and I am willing to leave the matter to the sterlingly honest judgment of the minister. When he applies that judgment -and there is no other man in the House in a better position to apply a business judgment than he-I am sure he will come to the conclusion that the people of New Brunswick have been unjustly treated in the matter, and that we should have that track replaced and be given back the connection and the right to do business, which we had before this track was taken away from us.

speakeroldname: Hon. FRANK COCHRANE (Minister of Railways and Canals):

speechtext:
This siding was
put in for the use of the contractors in the construction of the Transcontinental. To throw a different light on what my hon. friend has stated, I may say that * the Canadian Pacific railway have a station and sidings at Plaster Rock, where this spur joins their line. On the Transcontinental railway it was never intended to have a station or a siding at this point. This was only a temporary affair built by the Transcontinental Commission long before I had anything to do with the matter. One can understand the difference between transferring cars from the Canadian-Pacific railway, where there is a station and a siding, for the construction of the Transcontinental, and transferring cars from the Transcontinental to the Canadian Pacific railway where you would have to leave part of the train on the main line of the Transcontinental and push the cars up a steep grade to the Canadian Pacific railway. It is not a proper place for a transfer; and I am satisfied that if the road was under the control of the Railway Commission, they would neither authorize nor permit a transfer there under existing conditions. I do not want to put the blame on my officials, because I was a party to the removal of the spur.

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext: I am sorry to hear it.

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend says it is a proper transfer. I do not pretend to be a railway man; but as long ago as May, 1913, an engineer who was on the Transcontinental road a't the time wrote to the then superintendent, Mr. Brady, objecting, from the Transcontinental standpoint to this transfer. This is a question for an engineer, not for a layman like my hon. friend or myself. The letter is as follows:
May 31, 1913.
Dear Sir,-As no doubt you are aware, we now have two connections with the Canadian Pacific railway, Theriault at mileage 216, and Wabski at mileage 163.5. I would suggest that we abolish one of these points, and think that Wakski is the one that should be dropped, for the reason that we have to take our loads three quarters of a mile down a 2 per cent grade, with the risk of their getting away from us* and take the empties up the same grade. With the motive power we have had so far, our train has been frequently delayed from one to two hours. Last winter we had very often as many as twenty cars to lift at a time, and that meant four trains down the hill.
He is an engineer whose judgment I think my hon. friend will accept.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext: Who is he?

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext:
Mr. H. B. Dibblee. I understand that my hon. friend some years ago recommended this engineer to the Commission, although I have no evidence as to that. From all I know, he is a good engineer; and I am quoting him rather than my own engineers employed at Moncton, who also take the position that this is a dangerous point for a transfer. For the justification of myself and of the management at Moncton, I may say that we would rather haul the freight the whole distance to Fredericton for the rate that we receive than have our employees down there run the risk of losing their lives. I am willing at any time to remove any dangerous point and to overcome the difficulty in some other way, even at a loss of money. To overcome the opposition of shippers to the proposed removal of this transfer on account of the difference in mileage to Fredericton or Theriault, which would replace Wabski, the rates accruing to the National Transcontinental railway were so adjusted as to minimize the increase in the through rates; and if for the shorter haul from Fredericton the Canadian Pacific railway would make the rates to New England correspond with those which they apply from Theriault, the aggregate through charges against the

1G5
shippers of forest products originating on the Transcontinental would be the same.
In view of the temporary operation of the Transcontinental, we have not been in a position to quote or arrange for through freights. We are greatly handicapped, because we have no outlets ourselves and unfortunately we connect largely with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, who have absolute control in many cases. We hope to overcome this as soon as the money markets will allow us, so that we may be able to give the people of New Brunswick two outlets to the markets to the south.
The rate from Juniper to Wabski was four cents, as rightly quoted by my hon. friend, but that four cents did not pay us, because we had no siding at Wabski. We had to leave part of our train on the line in order to shunt up to the station four or five cars at a trip. On the other hand, the Canadian Pacific railway could leave their train on the siding and take the cars down.
The distance from Juniper to Fredericton is seventy-two miles, and we have made the rate four and a half cents. Therefore the freight, instead of being fifty cents, is only seventeen and a half cents per thousand feet of spruce, or 3,300 lbs., according to my hon. friend. In order to meet the hon. gentleman's clients and the general public, rather than take the risk of this dangerous interchange between the two railways, we would haul the freight from Juniper to Fredericton; and, on the whole, I think we would make more money as well as protect our employees by not making this dangerous transfer. The trains running to Fredericton could drop the cars off at a siding much more quickly than the locomotives could shove the cars for three-quarters of a mile up the hill.

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext: What does the minister now say is the rate from Fredericton to Boston points?

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext: I am not giving that. I do not know it.

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext: I do; that is the trouble. Fredericton is one hundred miles nearer than Plaster Rock to Boston points.

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext: Then your complaint is not against the Intercolonial railway or the Transcontinental; it is against the Canadian Pacific railway. If we haul the freight one hundred miles nearer to the Canadian Pacific railway, they can surely give the same rates or a little less.

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext: The minister is all in error.

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext:
I am not; I think my hon. friend will find that I am correct. If that proposition will not do, we will take the freight from Juniper to Theriault for five cents, not for one and a half cents, as my hon. friend quoted. To prove that my statement is correct, I want to quote a letter written by the I. N. Chase Lumber Company, a New England customer of Mr. Welch, one of the shippers from Juniper. It is as follows:
We are in receipt of yours December 17 regarding rates on lumber in carload lots from Juniper to New England points and we are greatly obliged to you for this information, the rate from Fredericton to New England to be used for furtherance. We had nothing like this before and thi3 gives us an opportunity to route shipments to New Haven points at a comparatively flat rate with shipments off the Canadian Pacific railway.
I want to assume the blame to a large extent of having this taken out. The matter was discussed with me before it was done, and the danger to employees was laid before me, and I O.K.'d the proposal.

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext: I have been consulted by the Donald Fraser Lumber Company with reference to this siding at Wabski. I understand that they have a pretty difficult situation on account of this siding. The Minister says that there was danger at that siding on account of running the train down the grade. But I have known of the running of trains on that siding at Wabski. I understand that they never heard of an accident there. I understand that the Donald Fraser Lumber Company is under a serious handicap for lack of siding at that point. I wonder if the Railway Commission of Canada would not authorize a siding there from the Transcontinental to the Canadian Pacific railway, but I am told that the minister has made up his mind that there shall not be a siding at that place. I am sorry to hear that.

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext: But we will overcome that difficulty so far as these people are concerned. As soon as the bridge and railway are completed at St. Leonard's, we will have an outlet to our bow, and will take the stuff to St. Leonard's and exchange with either the Canadian Pacific railway, the Maine Central or whoever is building that road.

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext:
I know that as a matter of fact the National Transcontinental is not getting business that it might get on the line from Edmundston to Plaster Rock. There are lumbermen along that line who claim that they cannot get Intercolonial railway cars in which to ship their lumber. I have that

personally from the shippers themselves, who tell me that they use Canadian Pacific railway cars to ship their lumber. The minister says I am wrong; I am sorry to say that the hon. gentleman himself is wrong. I have approached Mr. Fleming, the superintendent of that division of the Transcontinental. I am told that it was the station agent at Edmundston who went over the Wabski siding to gather the facts about it, and I am sorry to say that he was not the proper man to collect that information and send a report. The officials at Moncton took it for granted that this report was all right, and Mr. Fleming, superintendent of this railway in my constituency, said to me that the decision arrived at by the officials *upon the report of this station agent was final. I am sorry that such a report should be made. It was even said that it would be of no use for me to go on with the matter, -because everything was settled. I am glad that in the near future the international bridge will be built at St. Leonard's, and we shall have better communications. Meantime the Transcontinental railway is certainly not living up to its op-
5 p.m. portunities in the province of New Brunswick. A great traffic is possible in the district through which this railway runs, but there have arisen these difficulties in making the connections with the Intercolonial railway and Temis-couata railways. I hope that for the future we shall have better communications and better operation of the road. I do not wish to criticise the minister, but I must say that on some parts of the line the people are not satisfied with the officials of the railway, but little heed seems to be paid to the opinion of the people in this matter.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (North Cape Breton) :
subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext:
I trust the minister will pardon me if I take advantage of this discussion on the management of the Intercolonial railway to bring to his notice again two matters on which we have had some correspondence. He is aware that there is a change in the line of the railway in the eastern part of Cape Breton, between the towns of Sydney Mines and Florence and the city of Sydney. The road runs by a new route for a distance of ten or twelve miles, and for the first time the towns of Florence and Sydney Mines are on the main line of the Intercolonial railway. While the road was not placed exactly where, on business principles, it should be, we are satisfied for the present that the change is a great improvement on the old condition. What I wish particularly to bring to the minister's notice is the fact

that though the town of Florence is a mining and commercial town of about fifteen or sixteen hundred people where considerable business is transacted, yet the regular train does not stop there. There is a very good passenger station and freight shed, all new. The minister will understand what a startling surprise it was to the people of the town to find that the express train did not stop there. It is unnecessary for me to point out how inconvenient it is for the people that, though they have a railway station in their own town, they must go to Sydney Mines or to the Bras d'Or station to get aboard a train. I brought this to the minister's attention a month or five weeks ago, and he replied very promptly that he had asked the officials to take the matter into consideration. I have been watching from day to day to see what was to be done, in fact, to see the trains stop at this important point. But nothing has been done. I hope the minister will see to it that the people of Florence are given the full benefit of the road. It was bad enough to be inconvenienced when the road was not running that way but now that the road passes the doors of the people, it does seem an unusual thing in the history of the Intercolonial railway that trains do not stop at a place of this size and importance.
Another matter I have to inquire about is the local connection between Sydney and the points in the northern part of the county. The minister is aware that in very cold weather the ice stops our ferry. We are then dependent for communication between the city of Sydney and the northern part of the county on the local trains of the Intercolonial railway. For years that connection has been satisfactory, but this year the old traditions have been set aside and there are no regular trains, but we have to depend upon freights passing through.

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext: That train is running now.

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext:
It is only two days
since I got a letter -on the subject. There may have been improvements since, and if so there is no purpose in what I am saying. My information is that the regular train is not on, but if the minister says that the old service is restored, that is satisfactory.

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext: I am speaking only of the local train which runs there when the ferry stops. Do none of the trains stop at Florence?

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext:
None but freight trains.
I do hope this matter will be taken up at once and proper accommodation afforded the people of Florence. If the old conditions with regard to the local trains were re-established that would be quite satisfactory, but my information is that the old conditions did not prevail after the ferry stopped this year.

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext: I have not before me the information with regard to Florence, as I did not know that the matter would be brought up to-day. I was informed on Friday that the local train which operates when the ferry service is discontinued is now running. In any ease I shall certainly be glad to obtain information with regard to Florence, and to see what can be done.

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext: With the minister's permission, I wish to call his attention to a matter about which I have spoken to him privately: that is, the cancelling of a train previously running on what is known as the short line railway. The regular accommodation train is due in Pictou at 9.30 a.m. and, under the new arrangement, leaves at 11.40 a.m. A local paper says that on the four days during which the train had been in operation, owing to the extra work imposed upon it by reason of the taking off of the special it did not arrive in Pictou until about the time it was scheduled to leave. If the minister would extend the time of departure say to 1.30 p.m., the trainmen *would probably be later in reaching their destination at the other end, but the people would be enabled to get into the county town, transact their business and return the same day. May I have the assurance of the minister that he will look into this matter?

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext: Yes; I have made a note of it.

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext:
The minister has read a letter from the Chase Company of New York with regard to New York and New Haven points. I happen to know that the combined rates from Juniper to New York and New Haven points are not at all the same as the rate to Boston points, but I am not sufficiently acquainted with the details to discuss the matter intelligently. I wish the minister to remember, however, that it costs our company 18J cents to get that material from Juniper to Boston, via Fredericton, and 18i cents to get it to Boston by way of Theriault, while under the old arrangement we could get it to
Boston for 17 cents. These are the things the minister cannot get away from.

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext:
Your grievance is
against the Canadian Pacific railway.

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext: No; the Canadian Pacific railway have their rate, and they will maintain it, so far as I know. I have tried at various times to induce the Canadian Pacific railway to cut their rates, but I never succeeded in getting them to do so. As a matter of fact, I succeeded only once in my life in getting the Canadian Pacific railway to change their rates, and that was a case of getting them not to lower them but to raise them. I had no trouble in getting them to raise the rate, the only condition being that I should agree to defend them before the Railway Commission if any one tried to have the rate cut down to its original figure. A Boston party did attempt to have the rate cut and I defended the company-successfully, I may say. That is the only success I ever had with the Canadian Pacific railway in that respect. It would be useless for me to ask the Canadian Pacific railway to reduce the rate from Fredericton to Boston; the minister knows that they would not do it. There is no use in mincing the matter; the minister knows quite well that in suggesting that I have the Canadian Pacific railway cut their rate, he is asking me to do what is impossible.

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext: No, I do not.

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext: Well, the minister has had something to do with freight rates, and he should know that I cannot have that rate reduced. The minister does know, however, that he can cairy out the agreement he made with me a year and a half oi two years ago, and that he can get that lumber to Boston for 17 cents per cwt. But that is only my own part of the matter; that does not touch the root of the question. If it were entirely my own affair, I am sure that I would not take up the time of the House in discussing it. The whole public is interested in this outrage. My hon. friend says that we have no siding at the junction point. That may be true, but it would not cost very much to put a siding at the junction point; besides, my hon. friend must take the bitter with the sweet. If he is going to run a transportation company he must supply the people of Canada with transportation. It cannot be all cream; there must be some skim milk in the transaction.

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext: Cream for the Canadian Pacific railway, but none for the people of the country.

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext:
It cannot be all cream for my hon. friend. In one respect I think the minister has hardly been fair in his discussion of this matter. I do not say that offensively, because the minister always tries to be courteous, with me at any rate. Perhaps it has not occurred to him that the distance from that junction point to his station at Plaster Rock is not more than a mile and a half. The minister has a station on the north side of the Tohique river, with enough yard room to hold a great many more cars than he will handle on the road for a good many years, especially if he allows the thing to run as it is running at the present time. When the minister puts forward as an excuse the absence of sidings or yard room, I think he is putting up a severe form of special pleading. It is like a drowning man grasping at a straw; I think my hon. friend will get very little protection from his suggestion in that regard.
The matter, then, reverts back to the main question: does the minister want to give the people of that portion of New Brunswick the rights to which they are entitled, or does he not ? I am very sorry indeed to hear my hon. friend say that he does- not propose to put back the connection. That is what I understood him to say; if I am wrong, he has an opportunity of correcting me. I repeat that I am sorry indeed to hear him say so, because, unfortunately, when my hon. friend puts his foot down, it usually stays down. Possibly, however , my hon, friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries may be able to bring sufficient persuasion-I shall not say influence-to bear on my hon. friend the Minister of Railways to induce him to have the matter straightened out.
Did I understand the minister to say that in so far as my company is concerned, he will haul this freight to Boston at the same rate that it cost us before ? I thought I heard him say so.

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext: No, I did not. I said that our rate would give you a shorter mileage.

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext:
Then that grievance is not remedied; I thought my hon. friend would give me that assurance. My friend is in error as to the mileage. I am within a mile or two of being correct. It is not one hundred miles, but only about sixty-four from Plaster Rock to Boston than 
from Fredericton to Boston. McAdam Junction is a point common to both reads. As I figure it, it is one hundred and twenty-seven miles from Plaster Rock to McAdam and sixty-six miles from Fredericton to McAdam; that leaves a distance of about sixty-one miles against Plaster Rock. My hon. friend knows that the distance is not the only factor in the determination of freight rates; it is the competition that counts, the endeavour to get business at competitive points, and the fact that the Canadian Pacific railway are giving a lower rate from Plaster Rock and Theriault to Boston than from Fredericton to Boston is no fault of mine. It would not be that way if I could help it, but I am powerless.

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
