speechtext: It is not our fault.

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext: It is not mine and it is my friend who is making my company and every other man doing business along that road lose money. I can only say again that I am sorry my hon. friend has flatly refused to remedy this grievance. But I hope that, even at this late date, some influence or compulsion will be brought to bear on my hon. friend which will cause him to relent and give back to the people the right so ruthlessly taken from them.	.

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext: I wish to impress the hazardous nature of the operation of making that transfer; that is the reason for our taking out the connection.

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext: That is surely not a reason.

subtopic: I CL. RY.-FREIGHT RATES AND TRAINS.
speechtext: It is to me. When these men are under my charge we will not ask them to do a hazardous thing day after day Tf we can avoid it.
Motion agreed to.

speakeroldname: Mr. I. B. CARVELL (Carleton, N.B.,) moved:
speechtext:
For a copy of all letters, telegrams and correspondence had by Margaret Lynch, or any person representing her, with reference to the expropr iation of certain land belonging to the said Margaret Lynch in the city of Fredericton, province of New Brunswick, by the Intercolonial railway, and also of all letters, telegrams and correspondence had with F. P. Gutelius or any other official of the Intercolonial railway with reference thereto.
He said: This is very largely a private and professional transaction, but yet the matter has been so grossly handled that I -feel I am justified in calling the Minister's

attention to it in this public manner. I have done so privately, that is, by letter, and the minister, I think, did all he could, but unfortunately that was not enough to produce results. That is my justification for this motion. The minister is aware that, some time in the summer of 1913. the Department of Railways and Canals saw fit to expropriate quite a large lot of land in Fredericton belonging to a Mrs. Lynch. While, of course, the Minister of Railways has the legal right to expropriate any land, yet some discretion and respect for the rights of owners should be exercised. Mrs. Lynch is the owner of perhaps the finest residential grounds in Fredericton. It is the old residence of exGovernor Wilmot, one of the great men of New Brunswick, and it has been in the Lynch family a great many years. It consists of some ten or twelve acres. The old residence is a fine home surrounded by many beautiful shade trees. It is one of the most desirable properties in Fredericton, and that is saying a great deal because there is perhaps no town in Canada with more desirable places in it than Fredericton. The St. John and Quebec railway, commonly known as the St. John Valley Raliway Company, wanted a certain amount of this land for right of way sidings, warehouses, and generally in connection with their scheme. The railway company have never tried to purchase this land from Mrs. Lynch. An agent in Fredericton, who we understood was acting on behalf of the St. J ohn and Quebec Railway Company, wanted to buy the property from her two or three years ago. It was a private transaction, but nothing came of it. The next thing we knew the Intercolonial railway had filed plans to expropriate it. I have been prying into the affairs of the St. John and Quebec Railway Company during the past six or eight months and have got quite a bit of information in reference to it. I found in some of my excursions along that line that the St. John and Quebec Railway Company would have had to pay Mrs. Lynch for the land before taking possession, because if they took the land under the ordinary expropriation proceedings, under the Railway Act, they would be compelled to either buy it from this lady and pay her price or apply to the Court and deposit in Court such sum as the judge under such conditions might think fair and equitable. It seems that by getting my hon. friend to take charge of the matter for them they got rid of this inconvenience. They were able to get this land
without asking the owner for leave or license, they simply filed a plan in the office of the registrar of deeds and sent her avnotice that they had taken three or four acres of herjand. The next thing she knew a gang of navvies were on her land cutting down trees, tearing up the lawns and destroying the place; and when she protested they said: Well, what have you to say about it? We have the right, the Minister of Railways can do it. And when she said: I want my pay, they said: Go to the Minister of Railways and get your pay That was in 1913. I took the matter up for her, as her solicitor, and I attempted to get some sort of settlement with the Department of Railways and Canals, but I was put off and put off and put off. The ostensible reason given me at that time was that they might want more land and did not want to expropriate until they decided what land they wanted to take. They did take more land in the summer of 1914, a year afterwards; they filed another plan and made greater incursions upon her private property, cut down more shade trees, and reduced the value of the remainder of her property. They made her house, almost uninhabitable.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
How near do they go to
the house?

They go, I would say,
within 100 feet speaking generally. I will send the plan over to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, because he knows the property very well. He knows where those beautiful fir and elm trees were. They are practically all cut down. The line runs from a point on Regent street in a diagonal direction right back of the house. It would probably be more than 100 feet from the house to the line of the railway, but the land taken is really in the rear of the house. I wrote a number of letters to Mr. Gutelius and, I am sorry to say, there as in another matter, to which I referred this afternoon, and I did not get the courtesy of a reply, and could get no answer or satisfaction whatever. I realized that as a lawyer the Crown had a right to take this woman's property, but while I realized that the Crown had that right, there was also the moral right to try and settle with her or otherwise to start proceedings in the Exchequer Court to fix the compensation that should be allowed her. All I asked Mr. Gutelius to do was to either settle with this lady or to apply to the Exchequer Court and have compensation fixed. He would do neither. So again I resorted to a course

which I find generally produces results and 1 appealed to the minister. I have not the correspondence here but the minister, 1 have no doubt, has it. I have pointed out the condition of affairs to the minister. I know I used fairly strong language. I think I told him that they were acting as-I have just forgotten the exact word and I would not like to use one for fear it might be a little too harsh-but at all events the language I used was not very complimentary. I realized that they had a right to take that woman's property, but they ought to pay for it or go to court and have the compensation settled. I got back at once a very nice letter from the minister and I got action on the part of Mr. Gutelius so that the minister again did exactly what he should have done.
Some week or two after I wrote to the minister I received an offer from a very reputable firm of solicitors in Fredericton who were acting as agents of the Government, but as the offer was afterwards withdrawn 1 do not feel like making it public. It was a very respectable offer. Unfortunately, Mb's. Lynch was away in New York at the time and I was unable to give an answer immediately although I did not think she would have accepted the offer as it was not high enough but it was a reasonable offer coming from the Department of Railway and Canals. The amount was as large as we would expect the Department of Railways to offer when the Intercolonial railway is presided over by the gentleman who is the general manager of that institution at the present time because his heart is not known to have any great enlargement excepting when it comes to the question of his own salary. We have not seen any contraction whatever of the valve of that gentleman's heart when it comes to taking money out of the coffers of the Dominion of Canada, but we have seen every evidence of the most sudden contraction when that gentleman is paying money to other people of Canada whose property he is taking away from them. Under these circumstances, and coming from this gentleman, I thought it was a very reasonable offer.
Before my client returned to Fredericton, where I had been for three or four weeks attending court, the solicitors to whom I have referred came and asked me if I would be willing to give up the offer I had received in writing as they had received instructions from Moncton to withdraw it. As we have always got along in a very friendly way, I, as a matter of professional courtesy, gave

back the offer, and, as far as the legal effect of the matter is concerned, it stands as though the offer had never been made. From that day to this nothing has been done. They have taken altogether five acres of this lady's home. They have taken land that is worth a great many thousands of dollars, and they have torn up her property with the most ruthless hand possible. I have begged them now for a year and a half to start proceedings in the Exchequer Court. Let us have a judge of the Exchequer Court settle the matter, let them pay this woman what he says she is entitled, to and we will get satisfaction. But we can neither get the Department of Railways and Canals to pay us nor can we get them to put us into the Exchequer Court, and I do not know, from the manner in which this matter is being dealt with, that Mrs. Lynch may not be able to go to the Department of Justice-and get a fiat in order to bring suit against the Crown. I cannot believe that the Minister of Railways and Canals is going to stand for any such conduct as that.
I cannot believe that the minister wants to take people's property in the high-handed and barbarous manner I have detailed, giving them neither compensation for their property nor the chance to have the compensation settled by the proper authorities.
I know my legal rights, of course, as well as any lawyer in this House does. I know that my client can apply to the Minister of Justice and get a fiat to start suit against the Crown, but I also know that this involves an enormous expense. It is the duty of the Crown, when they take any person's land, to start proceedings in the Exchequer Court to ascertain the compensation to be allowed for the land taken. Why the Department of Railways and Canals are carrying on this affair as they are I cannot/understand. I have tried to figure it out m my own mind, but I am at a loss every time I try to do so.
I can understand quite well why the St. John and Quebec Railway Company did not go on. They would have been compelled to have paid the money before they got possession of the land, or to have paid a certain amount into court before they took possession, and that meant paying out money. We know that the St. John and Quebec Railway Company have not been very flush of funds for some time. But not so with the Department of Railways and Canals. Why you have taken this highhanded method without giving us a chance to find out what should be paid to us as compensation is something I cannot understand. While this is to some extent a

private transaction, yet it is a matter of so much importance that 1 feel compelled to bring it before the minister in this public manner, and all I ask is that he settle with us or bring us into court and allow the "proper tribunal to settle the matter and let us get our compensation and be done with it. That is a reasonable proposition, one that I do not think the minister will deny is reasonable, and now that I have brought it to his attention, I feel sure that he will be willing to see that the proper machinery is put in motion, that no more clogs are placed in the wheel, and that this woman shall be accorded the right to which she is entitled as a British subject and a person whose land has been taken by the Crown while no compensation has been made.

speakeroldname: Hon. FRANK COCHRANE (Minister of Railways and Canals):
speechtext:
When I took charge of the department I found that thgre was a system in reference to the acquisition of real estate which had been in vogue on the Intercolonial railway for a long time. About six months ago I became so disgusted with it that I issued a new order with reference to the matter, and it requires that we must get two or three men to value property which we wish to acquire. To give you a fair illustration of what I mean, let me say that at a certain place on the Intercolonial we wanted to put in a track scale. We saw the owner of the property which would best suit the purpose of the railway,	and	he	offered	to letus have	what	we	required	for	$80.
In conformity with this system we appointed three arbitrators, and instead of eighty dollars they assessed us six hundred dollars, and that puts us in the awkward position of having evidence piled up against us if we take it to the Exchequer Court. I would cite another instance: We wanted to acquire a certain property and the owner only asked $2.25 a foot for it, but we appointed three arbitrators and they charged us $800 for expenses, for a secretary and everything else, and they assessed it at three dollars a foot. In these circumstances, I concluded it would pay the department to get a valuator of our own who would have no axe to grind and who would give us.a fair valuation, and if the owners were not satisfied with it, they could go to the Exchequer Court. My hon. friend (Mr. Car-vell) has stated that this property was for the Quebec and St. John railway. The first expropriation was not for the Quebec and St. John railway, but for the Intercolonial railway, for a freight-shed and track which
we needed, because of the changing of the station, and its area was 3.81 acres.
I do not think it makes very much difference as to that.

It does, because it
removes some of the ground on which my hon. friend based his remarks.
Suppose the Quebec and St. John railway had never been built, would the minister have expropriated that land?

Yes, I would. The
hon. member stated that this property was 100 feet from the residence, but I have a plan here which shows it was 200 feet from Mrs. Lynch's residence.
That is all wrong.
I do not think so. It is quite a distance.
About fifty feet.
It is more than that.
At any rate, it is near her residence and you tore down her trees and cut through her summer house.

We had three men
value this property, and the value that was placed on the 3-81 acres was $11,935, or $3,132 per acre, and in the case of the second expropriation the land had an area of 1 -15 acres. The total valuation made by these gentlemen was $15,575.
You made no such offer as that to me.
No, because we considered it was altogether too large, and we believe so to-day.

We are convinced to
the contrary.

The lawyer who is
handling the case for the Intercolonial railway is a gentleman of some repute, Mr. R. B. Hanson, and he protested against it. He says in a letter:
August 27, 1914.
Replying to your favour of the 26th instant, I beg now to give you some of my reasons for considering that the property taken from Mrs. Lynch is not worth more than 58,000 or $9,000. The Intercolonial railway takes approximately five acres of this property but only a portion of the part taken is on a streft. tit' bilanc is inaccessible at present and will be for the future unless the street is put through. There was no prospect of a street until after the Intercolonial had expropriated and built the freight

shed. The property immediately across Regent street, known as Scully's Grove, contains 14 acres. It is situated in as good a position, in fact better, as it had access not only to Regent street, but also St. John street, and it sold in 1911 or thereabouts for $10,000, for the whole block, and the executor of the estates thinks he made a splendid sale and so do I. A few years before (not more than three or four) the estate of Wm. H. Scully sold the same property to Charles Scully for $4,000. This was a bargain, of course, but it is also a fact to be taken into consideration.
The Randolph property, known as ' Frogmore,' situate on the same side of Regent street, but west of the Canadian Pacific railway, contains
22 acres. It has a fine residence, stables and outbuildings, with fine graded grounds and large gardens and fields, and could have been purchased at any time during the last four or five years for $18,000 at the outside.
The value of the land alone taken by the Intercolonial railway considered as a whole, having in view the uses to which it could be put before August, 1913, would not, in my opinion, exceed $1,000 per acre, which would aggregate, in the whole, about $5,000. The damages to the property adjacent are difficult to measure; the conditions have not changed. A railway ran along the edge of her property then. A railway runs along the edge of her property now. The only difference is that the railway which skirts her property now is some distance nearer her residence than it was in 1913. Without pretending to estimate all the consequential damages, I would think that $3,000 or $4,000 would be liberal.
I understood also that an offer of $13,500 was made to my hon. friend (Mr. Carvell), but he refused it. I am not in a position to prove that, but I give the statement for what it is worth.
Do you want me to answer that P
I am not making any assertion about it.
I may say that Mr. Hanson who gave me the offer gave it to me in writing, and I wish to state here that Mr. Hanson and I are the very best of personal friends.
I understand so.

At that time I was acting as counsel with Mr. Hanson in a very large expropriation. I never saw my client and had no opportunity to, as she was away in New York. Three days afterwards, Mr. Hanson asked me if I would give to him the offer that had been made, as he had received instructions' from Moncton to that effect, and as a matter of professional courtesy I handed it back.
You did not refuse it or accept it ?
I had not the opportunity; I had not seen my client.
I accept your word.
Mr. Hansen will bear out what I say.

I will see that there is no further delay in sending the case to the Exchequer Court. I do not want to say that those men who valued the property have not acted fairly, but the man whom we sent down there agreed with Mr. Hanson as to the value, and he thinks he can sustain his opinion in the^Ex-chequer Court.

Would the minister give me the names of the gentlemen who valued this land ? I understood there had been some gentlemen appointed 'but we never knew the result of their valuation until to-day, and it is interesting.
I do not think I ought to give the names. We will try to prove that their opinion is right.
The minister does not want to give me the names ?
I would rather not.

They will be given in the court, and the minister might as well give them now. I do not think the minister has grasped the pointjf was trying to make. The fact is that great damage has been done to this lady's property. I will send to the minister a photograph showing what he has destroyed. You may talk about the Germans ravaging Belgium, but there has been nothing worse done in Belgium than the minister has done in this case.
I know all about it. I was on the ground before the expropriation.

I am sending the minister a photograph of the ground he lias cut up and run his railway through, and I wish I could get the photograph on "Hansard". It is not a question, however, how much damage has been done to my client's property. We will take our chances of convincing the Exchequer Court as to how much damage has been done. It is not a question of how much was paid for Scully's grove, because that is a matter for the courts to find out. Scully's grove is a baseball field on the opposite side of the street and a little farther towards the Canadian Pacific Railway tracks.
It is good commercial property.
Yes. It has not a building on it; I do not think it ever had. It has been used as a baseball field and as a general resort for athletes. I think it was sold for $7,000, as Mr. Hanson states.

The railway runs
alongside of the property which we have taken and it would not be residential property.

I admit that Mrs. Lynch does not reside on every inch of this land, but it is all enclosed by her fences. It is land she did not want to sell to a railway company; she was holding it for other purposes; it is land which, as I said before, was probably the best residential property in Fredericton. It was formerly occupied by Governor Wilmot. Mrs. Lynch did not want a railway within 150 feet of her residence. When my hon. friend speaks about comparing the quantity of land taken with the Scully grove property, he is speaking as many railway people do when they take away people's land-they simply speak of acreage. Were I sitting as a judge of the [DOT]Exchequer Court, the last thing I would consider in giving damages would be acreage. The acreage, the actual land taken, is the last thing which an arbitrator should consider. It is the damage done to the rest of the property that counts.
Frogmoro, to which my hon. friend has referred, is nearly half a mile away from Mrs. Lynch's property.
That is better residential property.

No, it is not. It is away out in the country. You have to cross the Canadian Pacific railway track and climb a hill in order to get to it. There is no comparison whatever. You could cut up the Lynch property into lots to-morrow, and you could sell every one of them in the course of two or three years. If you were to cut up the Frogmore property into lots, you could not sell them in twenty-five years, because the city of Fredericton is not growing rapidly enough. That, however, is a matter which we shall discuss when it comes to the court. The point is that my hon. friend has taken this woman's property, and he will not pay her nor put her into court.
I will put her into court.

I hope my hon, friend will; that is all we ask. We shall be satisfied with what we get. If we cannot get more than $15,000 damages, or more than $7,000, the value that my hon. friend's solicitor puts on the property, I shall be much surprised. I think my hon. friend's solicitor has had his eyes opened. He is learning a lot of law on the right side of these arbitration cases; that is, the side of the owner, the person whose property has been damaged. If my hon. friend would write again to his agent, he would get a somewhat different valuation from what he got three months ago.

I have not received
any.

My hon. friend should
write to his agent again. I know the gentleman very well, and his mind has had a wonderful transformation during the last few months as regards the potential damage to property and the amount of damage that ought to be allowed for taking the land itself for severance and all those other matters that enter into the question of damages in an arbitration or Exchequer court suit. As I have my hon. friend's promise that he will put this matter into the court, that is all I want, and we will undertake, to look after the law of it and try to see that the lady gets the amount of compensation to which she is entitled.

Motion agreed to.
At six o'clock, the House took recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

speakeroldname: Mr. F. B. CARVELL (Carleton, N. B.) moved:
speechtext:
For a copy of all letters, telegrams, correspondence, contracts, and other documents relating to the operation of the St. John Valley railway, so called, by the Intercolonial railway, since the first day of July last past, and of all letters, correspondence, etc., had either with the Department of Railways and Canals, or with F. P. Gutelius, or any other official of the Intercolonial railway.
He said: Before this motion is passed, I desire to recall to the attention of the minister what we look upon in New Brunswick as the very unfair attitude assumed by the Department of Railways and Canals in the operation of the Valley railway, so called. While it may be possible that the minister is technically within his rights and is not compelled to do more than he is doing, yet, if he be right, it is the narrowest, most

technical construction of a statute and contract I have ever known since I entered Parliament. He agreed in the most solemn fashion imaginable, and this Parliament by statute provided, that if the province of New Brunswick built a certain road up to a certain standard-a standard set by the minister himself-and did certain other things, he would operate that road as part of the Intercolonial railway, and pay back to the province forty per cent of the gross earnings with which to pay interest on the bond guarantee, the 'balance, if any, to go to the company that built the road. Now, I am not here as the special champion of the Government of the province of New Brunswick, nor of the company that built the road. I have had occasion during the last three or four years to say' many things which were perhaps not entirely complimentary both to the Government and to the company. But the people of the province of New Brunswick have certain rights and privileges; they have a future before them, and they have certain debts which they must pay. Therefore, I contend, the Minister of Railways and Canals should carry out this contract made in good faith with the province of New Brunswick, whether he has the most friendly feeling towards the Government of New Brunswick and the railway company or not. This is a question bigger, broader and much more important than whether the province of New Brunswick has carried out its contract or whether the company has acted in perfect good faith. This is a matter that has caused great discussion in New Brunswick during the last two or three years; in fact, it has been one of the greatest bones of political contention we have had there since 1909. The subject has been discussed in this House many times, and I am not going over it now except to say generally that the people wanted a railway built along the river St. John through a country portions of which had been settled for a hundred years and which was without railway communication. This section contained some of the finest and most productive land of Canada, yet some parts of it were thirty and forty miles away from railway communications. Portions of this area had water communication during seven months of the year, but others had not even that. The great need was the need of railway communication. For some reason which I can hardly explain-and it does not matter for my present purpose-when the railways in western New Brunswick were built, they 
did not follow the St. John river below Woodstock. A branch line ran into Fred. ericton, but in the whole distance of one hundred and forty miles this point, Fredericton, about equi-distant from Woodstock and St. John, was the only point that had railway communication with the outside world. After years of agitation and, I am bound to say, considerable cross-firing between the Government of New Brunswick and the Government of the Dominion, what we thought a fair working basis was arrived at which was embodied in legislation passed in the session of 1911. Among the provisions of that statute were the following.
The Governor in Council is authorized to enter into a contract with any ra iway company already authorized, or which may hereafter be authorized by law, to construct a line of railway from a point on the line of the National Transcontinental at Grand Palls, in the county of Victoria, to the city of St. John, in the province of New Brunswick, a distance of about two hundred and twenty miles, the principal and interest of the bonds of which railway company, pursuant to the provisions of chapter 6, of the statutes of the province of New Brunswick, 1910, the Government of the province of New Brunswick has guaranteed, or may guarantee, to the extent of twenty-five thousand dollars per mile, and with the Government of the province of New Brunswick, for the leasing of the said line of railway when completed, with its appurtenances, and for its operation, equipment, maintenance, up-keep and repair by the Government of Canada, as part of the Government railway system of Canada, for a period of ninety-nine years and for the payment by the Government of Canada to the said province of New Brunswick, or to the said company, each year during the said term ninety-nine years, of forty per centum of the gross earnings of the said railway as or in the nature of rental thereof:	Provided, howtvr. that
the said contract shall be entered into only upon the condition that the said railway shall be constructed upon plans and specifications to bo approved of by the Governor in Council upon the recommendation of the Minister of Railways and Canals and shall be up to the general standard of the said National Transcontinental railway through the said province: Provided further that the Governor in Council shall be authorized to enter into a contract, as aforesaid, for the operation of the said railway in sections, when completed and equipped, as follows:
(1)	Prom Fredericton to Woodstock;
(2)	Prom Fredericton, south, a distance of fourty miles;
(3)	Each twenty-five miles, thereafter, until the line be completed from Grand Falls to St. John.
That is an important part of the statement, because it gives the minister the right to go on and operate the road. When tire present minister (Mr. Cochrane) came into office in October, 1911, he found the contract drawn up between the Dominion
FEBRUARY 15, 19i5
Government and the Provincial Government and the St. John and Quebec Railway Company which we thought was satisfactory to all parties concerned. I think it had been signed by the Dominion Government, though I am not really positive about that. However, it had not been signed by the Provincial Government. But it had been drawn up at the conference of the three parties concerned, who agreed that it would be sufficient. During the election of 1911 the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) and his colleague in the Government of New Brunswick had promised all over New Brunswick that within a feiv days they would sign the contract. But the elections came, the Dominion Government was defeated, and the contract had not actually been signed.
The next year, in the session of 1912, that legislation was repealed in so far as the practical working out of the scheme was concerned, and new legislation was passed which necessitated the making of a new contract. The difficulty occasioned by the new legislation was that it provided practically no specification upon which the road should be constructed.
If I may be permitted to anticipate the answer of the hon. minister, I think he will say: Oh, well, you have not given me as good a road as I wanted; you have not given me a road which I can operate economically and at the same time pay you back forty cents out of every dollar. I am not sure that the minister will not go further and take the extremely technical ground that the road is not completed, that these sections have not been constructed and completed according lu the statute and that, therefore, he is not compelled to operate it under the statute. I want to discuss in a very cursory manner these two phases of my hon. friend's answer-because I know that will be his answer-in order to show him the fallacy of the principle under wnich he is acting. If my hon. friend has not as good a road as he ought to have, it is his own fault. If the road is full of twists and curves and crooks and hills and everything that is contrary to good railroading, then he has only himself to blame. When my hon. friend came into office he found upon the statute book legislation which provided for the construction of a railroad. One of his first official acts in so far as railways in New Brunswick were concerned was to pass an Act repealing the legislation which provided for the construction of a good railroad, and to give his political friends in the province of New Brunswick the right to build anything-so long as it consisted of a roadbed and two rails-and pass it over to him as a railway. I am not going to say that as a railway, aside from the question of -curves and grades, it is not a pretty good railway; perhaps I shall not be charged either with egotism or with excessive modesty if I say the course I took last year had something to do with making the road as good as it is. We had a rather severe investigation into this matter in the province of New Brunswick during the last year. We had shown up a great many things which have not redounded to the credit of the party in power in New Brunswick; we have compelled them to spend a great many thousands of dollars which they never intended to spend. Taking it all round, we have a pretty good roadbed; the difficulty is that it is not a very good road upon which to do business, because of the curves and grades.
I want to point out to my hon. friend wherein he has to thank himself for the difficulties under which he is labouring this evening. Chapter 49 of the Statutes of 1912 recites in the first place that by Chapter 11 of the Statutes of 1911 this Parliament agrees to operate the road as part of the Intercolonial. It goes on to recite the general substance of the legislation of 1911, and then it provides for assistance towards the building of three big bridges. That I will refer to later. I do not believe my hon. friend the Minister of Railways realized for a moment the true significance of section 10 of this Act when it was being passed. I wish the Minister distinctly to understand that what I am saying to him to-night is not personal. I have no idea in the world that the Minister knew what he was doing -I do not say that offensively-but his friends, to use a slang phrase, put it all over him, and now he is compelled to pay the penalty. The first part of section 10 reads as follows:
Notwithstanding anything in any other Act, the agreement set out in the schedule to this Act is hereby ratified and confirmed and declared to be binding upon the respective parties thereto, subject to the provisions of this Act, and the Dominion may do whatever is necessary to give full effect to the said agreement and specifications and to the provisions of this Act.
My hon. friend will see that with one stroke of the pen everything done in 1911 was set aside; an entirely new contract was opened up and the Minister was bound to it. The schedule referred to in section 10

was an agreement which had previously-been entered into between this Government, the Government of the province of New Brunswick, and the St. John and Quebec Railway Company. The St. John-and Quebec Railway Company was a provincial organization having at its head a very shrewd American gentleman, Mr. A. R. Gould-a man who knows how to put it over my hon. friend, or my hon. friend's friends, without any difficulty whatever. This contract was made on the 5th day of March, and the legislation was not passed until the 1st day of April, 1912. The legislation of 1912 simply ratified this contract and made it the law of the land in the place and stead of the legislation of 1911. The contract first provided as follows:
Whereas it has been agreed by the several parties hereto that the said Company shall construct the said railway under and pursuant to an agreement which has heen entered into between the company and the province, dated December twelfth, one thousand nine hundred and eleven, whereby the said province agrees to guarantee first mortgage bonds of the said company to the extent of $25,000 per mile.
Then, the enacting part of the contract proceeds as follows:	.
Now this indenture witnesseth.
That the said company hereby undertakes and agrees that the said railway, including the line of railway and all bridges connecting the same or forming part thereof as in the first paragraph of the preamble of this agreement set out, or intended so to be, shall be constructed and equipped in all respects up to and according to the specifications hereto annexed.
My hon. friend agreed that all they had to do was to build the railway up to the specifications annexed to the contract, and his department would take it over, operate it for 99 years, and pay back to the province of New Brunswick 40 per cent of the gross earnings. But the trouble is that there are no specifications annexed to the contract.
There is a specification.
It is not here.
That may be.

I can go further than
that, and say that we have never been able to get the specifications. If they are or have been in existence, I should like to see them and ascertain what kind of agreement my hon. friend made at that time. Then subsection 2 of the contract provides:
That the company shall complete the construction and the equipment of the said railway in all respects up to and according to the specifications hereto annexed and the requirements

as in the preceding clause set out on or before the first day of November, in the year of Our Lord one thousand nine hundred and fifteen.
There again the specifications are kept secret so far as the public is concerned. To-day the people of New Brunswick and the people of Canada in general have no knowledge of what the specifications were or what kind of railway these people agreed to build for the minister. Subsection 9 of the contract is as follows:
It is hereby understood and agreed by and between all the parties hereto, that during the first fifteen years of the term of the said lease forty (40%) per cent of the gross earnings of the said railway (exclusive of the bridges) and the bridges shall be paid by the Government of Canada to the Province of New Brunswick to be applied so far as necessary towards payment of the interest upon the said bonds so to he guaranteed by the Province of New Brunswick, and the surplus, if any, after payment of said interest to he paid semi-annually to the railway company; and during the first fifteen years of the term of the said bridge bonds the interest thereupon shall be paid and borne by the Government of Canada as further aid towards the construction of the said bridges.
The substance of that legislation was this: The minister agreed that when they completed the construction of the railway according to the terms of the specification- which we do not know anything about- they would agree to take that road over and operate it in sections and when the road was completed he would take a leasehold of it and would pay back to the province of New Brunswick 40 per cent of the gross earnings with which to pay the interest on the bonds. That is the contract which the minister made. Acting on that, the railway company went to work in the spring of 1912 and have since built 120 miles of railway running from Centreville in Carle-ton to Gagetown in the county of Queens, passing through York and Sunbury. The first of the sections referred to in the statutes of 1911 to which I referred the minister before, was from Centreville to Woodstock. That road has been built from Fredericton to Woodstock and, according to my information, has been completed.
I received an answer from the minister the other day as to whether the contract had been carried out; he said the road was not completed. I hope the minister will say in what respect the road has not been completed. I wish to say it has been completed, that we had an inspector this year, Mr. J. J. Taylor, who, I believe, tried to do his duty, a gentleman who, while not satisfied with the specifications, yet held the

company down to those specifications as well as he could, a gentleman who certainly made that company do everything which he could possibly conceive he was entitled to make them do under those specifications. He could not make them cut out one per cent grades by the hundreds and seven degree curves by the dozen because these were in the specifications. I think that the first protest that came to the minister over the character of the road came from Mr. Justice Crocket, then Conservative member for the county of York. He made very severe protests against the number of seven degree curves and one per cent grades they were inserting but all of no avail. Mr. Taylor made not only one protest but tens and dozens, and I think I may say hundreds of protests against the character of the road they were building, but all of no avail. In every case he was turned down. When it came to questions of the quality of the culverts and the width of embankments, the amount of ballast, the character of ties and all such things as that, he had his own way and in so far as he was allowed to be the judge of the question. My hon. friend has as good a railway as it is possible to give him; but whenever it got beyond the power of Mr. Taylor, the politicians interfered and my hon. friend has a railway about which he complains to-day and over which he will complain that he cannot do business at a profit. That is his fault and not the fault of his inspecting engineer. I have endeavoured to find out, if I can, wherein the road is not completed between Fredericton and Woodstock-and I might say it is also completed from Woodstock north, a distance of twenty-five miles, and they treat the two together. I have tried to find out wherein the two sections are incomplete. I am assured by gentlemen who ought to know, by the officials of the railway company itself, that the only thing which is not completed on that section of nearly eighty miles of road is a track scale at Woodstock which I believe has not been placed. It may be that my hon. friend can technically say that because a track scale has not been put in in a stretch of railway eighty miles long, the road is not completed and he is not compelled to operate it; but if he takes that ground it is the most literal interpretation of a contract I have ever heard and one which will not please his friends or any other person in New Brunswick.
The next thing is that portion of the road from Fredericton south to Gagetown. I tell my hon. friend the road is completed from Fredericton to Gagetown, a distance of thirty-six miles, going through the counties of York, Sunbury and Queens; and I have it from thq contractor who built that portion of the road, I have it from the railway company itself, I have it from gentlemen who live along the line of the road, it is common knowledge in New Brunswick, that this part of the road also is absolutely completed excepting that there may be a little riprapping to be done along some of the track, but that is a matter which has been left in abeyance and which may or may not be required. The Minister must remember that, by the contract, if it becomes necessary to do anything else in the way of capital expenditure he has the power to do that work and charge it back to the company. So if it should turn out that there were any little matters not entirely completed the minister has the power to do the work and charge it back to the company and the Intercolonial suffers no loss from the transaction. What do you suppose will be my hon. friend's answer as to his reason for not operating that portion of the road. It is no more and no less than the fact that the contract says the road was to be forty miles in length and it is only thirty-six miles and they have a road entirely completed with no exceptionally bad grades except one, although the curves are not what they might be. The railway runs through a portion of the province which has been settled for over one hundred years. It is a country which has no communication whatever with the outside world in the winter. One of the finest producing countries of Canada and is to-day without railway accommodation; and yet it has a railway entirely completed, ready for operation and the Minister of Railways refuses to operate it because he said to the company; you agreed to build a stretch forty miles long and have only completed thirty-six miles. That is the only reason the Minister can urge for his non-operation of that section. When it comes to the other two sections of the road, that is from Fredericton north to Woodstock and from Woodstock north to Centreville, he cannot urge that the sections are not completed because the road is completed from Fredericton to Woodstock and is completed not twenty-five miles but twenty-six miles north of Woodstock. If my hon. friend tries to apply a somewhat hairsplitting interpre-



tation of the contract he might say: I will operate that road up to within one mile of Centreville and then stop because I have entered into a contract with relation to a line to a point twenty-five miles north and this is twenty-six miles. He is operating the twenty-six miles. He is running one train a way a day over the road from Centreville to Fredericton. I am not complaining so much of the character of the service he is giving. I realize that it is a new road and that it takes time to work up business; and while I would like to see a little better train service, I wish to be reasonable. I hope that in the future we will have a better service than at the present, but it is a great advantage over no train service at all. In the twenty-five miles from Woodstock to Centreville I believe the road will get more freight than can be obtainedjrom any other twenty-five miles of purely agricultural country in Canada, and that is saying a good deal. It may be that for the last two months the minister has not been getting as much traffic as he might expect because, unfortunately, a great portion of the traffic originating in that section is potatoes, and there is no market to-day for potatoes in Canada or elsewhere, and I believe there are to-day half a million barrels awaiting shipment there. If the time comes, and it must come, when we can find a market for these potatoes, we will find that the capacity of the road will be taxed to the utmost and what is true this year will be true next year and every year. I repeat that I do not believe the minister will find twenty-five miles of agricultural area in Canada that will produce more traffic of a purely agricultural character than this twenty-five miles of road.
But when it goes beyond Fredericton, while possibly it is not as good a country, and while there would not be as much traffic, yet these people have no accommodation whatever, simply because the minister says: You agreed to build a road forty miles long, and you have only completed thirty-six miles. Yet the thirty-six miles takes in the large and thriving town of Gagetown, the shire town, and if the minister insisted on going the other four miles he would simply be going down four miles into the country. There is no reason why the company should have built the section beyond Gagetown, because that will come in connection with the next section. I have no doubt that the company never had any idea that forty miles would be required to be built, or that the minister would take any exception if there were not the exact forty miles built.

Now the minister maintains that he is excused from operating that road because they have not complied strictly with the terms of the contract. I do not believe that his colleagues, that the Government, that his followers in the House, that anybody in the province of New Brunswick, will agree with him in the excuse which will be put up for the non-operation of that portion of the road. I not only condemn the minister here, to-night, for not operating that road, but I condemn him for not operating any portion of that road according to the contract. The minister-and when I use the word " Minister " I mean the Government, because I want to make it perfectly clear that I cast no personal reflection on the present incumbent of the office-has not carried out his bargain with the people of New Brunswick, with the Government of New Brunswick, or with the railway company. He agreed by chapter 49 of the Statutes of 1912, in the most solemn manner possible, that when that road was completed according to certain specifications, he would operate it and pay forty per cent of the gross earnings to the people of that province. He has not done that. He shakes his head as much as to say, I suppose, that he does not intend to.
I did not agree to it.
Did not agree to it? I have read the Statute.
Let me answer for myself; you need not answer.
I will try to let my hon. friend know what I want him to answer.
You are trying to give my answer.

And when I have done I will be perfectly willing to listen to the answer which my hon. friend wishes to give. I said he made a contract, and he has broken his contract with everybody concerned. As far as the Government of New Brunswick are concerned, it does not bother me very much whether they are in trouble or not, and as far as the railway company are concerned, it is perfectly clear that they are not clients of mine, but if everybody had carried out his contract the same as this company have, perhaps we would not be in the mess which we are in to-day. As far as the people of New Brunswick are concerned, the people who have to pay the interest on this enormous debt which has been rolled up over their heads, they are concerned, and it is for that reason that I am calling upon the minister to

explain why he has not carried out the contract.
This road was completed practically ready for operation, and should have been in operation, last October. I do not say it was completed in the sense that every spike was driven, every shovelful of ballast had been placed upon the road, or that the last brush of paint had been put upon the station houses, but I do say that way back even in September this road was completed and fit for traffic. The roadbed was entirely completed long before that, and it was perfectly feasible to operate the road in October. The produce of that country, which is largely potatoes, was saleable in very large quantities in September and October, and hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of potatoes grown in that country might have been gotten out if the minister had in an honourable spirit carried out the contract and operated the road. He did not do so, and the result is that this stuff is locked up to-day, there is no market for it, and I am afraid there will be no market for it. Today he is not operating the road according to his contract. I got an answer from him on Friday last, I think, and according to that answer no portion of the gross receipts of that road go to the province of New Brunswick. As I understand the contract says that no matter what the road earns, nothing goes to the province of New Brunswick.
I did not say that.
That is what I understood the hon. gentleman's answer to be.
No, I did not say that. You mean the present operation ?
The present operation.
There w;ll not be any.
I see; there will not be any other per cent. Am I right ? I think I have the faculty of understanding the English language when I read it.
I misunderstood your statement.

Whereas by the contract which Parliament made, the people of New Brunswick were to have forty per cent on every dollar earned, under the present agreement they get nothing; and, worse than that, the Intercolonial takes all, but if there should be a loss in operation, we pay half of the loss. What is the contract which my hon. friend made, or which Parliament made for him in 1912 ? I would like to know it. That is what I am find-124
ing fault with and that is what I want the minister to explain. Why should the people of New Brunswick be compelled to pay the interest on the bonds to something like three or four million dollars P We are liable to pay the interest on bonds to the amount of $4,000,000 and we are not getting one dollar out of the operation of the road with which to pay that interest, whereas, by the statute, by the contract made by Parliament, we are entitled to receive forty per cent of the gross earnings of the road with which to pay interest on the bonds. The minister may say: I do not think I am going to make money out of it. That is not the contract. He may say: You have not finished the road. That is not the contract. He may say: You have not built the kind of road you should have built. That is not the contract. He agreed, no matter what kind of a road we built, that he would operate it. He agreed that, so long as we built a section of 25 miles, he would take it over, and he agreed to take the whole of it. He agreed to pay forty per cent of the gross earnings for the purpose of assisting the people of New Brunswick to meet the interest on the bonds. These are things which the minister is called upon to answer. But he may say: Well, you agreed when the contract was made that you would finish that road to Grand Falls by the first of November, 1915. Let him quarrel with the people who made the contract, let him go to his friends the Government of New Brunswick, let him go to his friends of the St. John and Quebec Railway Company and ask them why they did not carry out their contract. But that is not the fault of the people of New Brunswick. It is not the fault of the men who have to pay the interest on those bonds. Just here perhaps my hon. friend may ask me whose fault it is. Why was that road not completed according to the contract ? It is all very simple. It has not been completed according to the contract because of the boodling, the worse than boodling, the almost pilfering of public money, by the men whose duty it was to safeguard the interests of the people of the province. He may say that if the road had been built through to Grand Falls he would have been able to get traffic from the Transcontinental railway and do a through business. It is not our fault that that has not been done. I have talked upon this question in the House a number of times. I have stated before, and I repeat to-night, that the road never was

justifiable. The whole scheme never was justifiable. The whole scheme was almost a business and political crime if it did not go through to Grand Falls and draw freight from the Transcontinental railway. The whole scheme was based on the idea that it was to be the outlet for transcontinental railway freight into the city of St. John, and without the transcontinental railway freight it was never feasible for a moment because there will not be sufficient traffic originating along that road, partly as a branch line of the Canadian Pacific railway, to give enough business to pay forty per cent on the bonds and yet leave sufficient margin to operate the road. It is, not the fault of the people that the road has not been built to Grand Falls. The minister's friends in New Brunswick may say to him: we cannot sell our bonds on account of the war and therefore we cannot extend the road to Grand Falls, but there never was a more unjust, unfair, and dishonest statement than that, and the minister's friends are simply deceiving him in the most scandalous manner possible-were it parliamentary to use a stronger term I would use it, but the minister can supply the term mentally without my saying it orally. The fact is that in 1912, when the money market was in splendid condition the province of New Brunswick and that railway company sold on the London market bonds for 170 miles at $25,000 a mile, and not for the 120 miles they intended to build. The actual cash brought from England, away back in May, 1912, amounted to $1,200,000, and that money is on hand or ought to be on hand from that day to this, and if it is not on hand to-day it is because some person in the province of New Brunswick, pretty close to the minister-

Do you mean to say
I got any of it?
No.

Or anybody in this House?
Mr. CARVELj. :	There is no question
about who is responsible; it is the Government of New Brunswick. They brought that money to Canada, and instead of putting it in the Bank of Montreal, in the Bank of Nova Scotia, or in the Royal Bank, or in one of the big trust companies, as they ought to do, they put it in the hands of a trust company in Montreal-with which I do not want to have any quarrel, and against which I have not a word of condemnation-that is at least not to be

compared with the big institutions to which I have referred. They put $4,000,000 in the hands of a company called the Prudential Trust Company, and the only qualification put upon the investment of that money was a letter written by the then Provincial Secretary of New Brunswick, the present member for York in this House (Mr. McLeod), addressed to the Prudential Trust Company, and telling them they were at liberty to invest that money as they thought fit, the only condition being that every three months they should send to the Government of New Brunswick a statement of the manner in which that money had been invested.
Now, if they have not got the cash to build that road, the fault lies with the Government of New Brunswick and the Prudential Trust Company. I do not want to go further; I do not think it would be fair to go further; I can only say that they cannot get the money, and they are putting it up to the people of the province as a reason why they cannot get the money, that the money market is in such a bad condition that they cannot sell their bonds. I think I am justified in the assertion I made a moment ago as to the word that ought to be used, when these people tell the minister that they cannot finish the road because they could not sell bonds to get the money.
Again, they may say to the minister: we have issued second mortgage bonds at ten thousand a mile and we cannot sell these second mortgage bonds. I tell the minister that it is not necessary to sell the second mortgage bonds. I tell him that if he can get the cash for the first mortgage bonds, or if the Government, or the Prudential Trust Company, or whoever has the money can dig up the money from the first mortgage bonds, I will find contractors who will take the second mortgage bonds upon their own responsibility and build the road. There is no trouble about that at all. The contractors who built the road from Woodstock to Centreville-I have no hesitation in giving their names, they are Kennedy & Macdonald of Antigonish, N.S., who were large contractors on the National Transcontinental-never received a dollar of the $10,000 a mile second mortgage bonds, but took the bonds themselves. The same is true of the Hibbard Company, which built the road from Fredericton to Woodstock, and the same is true of the Corbett Construction Company, which built the road from Fredericton to Gagetown. They took the second mortgage bonds of $10,000 a mile and financed them themselves.

I was solicitor for two of these companies, and I tell the minister they are perfectly willing to take these second mortgage bonds and to build the remainder of the road, providing they have the assurance that the money which ought to he in the hand's of the Prudential Trust Company is forthcoming. They will take that money and they will take these second mortgage bonds and they will build the road, and if the road is not finished it is not the fault of the contractors or anybody else, except the Minister's political friends in New Brunswick.
You may ask me why the money was put in the hands of the Prudential Trust Company. I will throw a little sidelight on the transaction, and only a sidelight, because I am not here to discuss everything that has been made public in New Brunswick during the past year. The Minister may say: Why did these men put that money in the place in which they did instead of in one of the big financial institutions of Canada? I can tell the Minister that there was a very good reason for it, a reason which was brought out in the investigation held in New Brunswick last year. We proved in that investigation that before the bonds were sold an agreement was made with the Prudential Trust Company that in case the money was left to them on deposit they would loan to Mr. Gould and his associates on their notes alone the sum of $350,000 which of course would come out of that trust fund. The money was brought from England in May, and between that date and the running of the provincial elections, $200,000 was paid over to Mr. Gould and his associates, on their own private notes. The notes were signed by Mr. A. R. Gould, a bright, shrewd, active Yankee promoter, who lives in the State of Maine a few miles away from where we live, by Ross Thompson, chief engineer of the road, by Mr. Lisman, a lawyer of New York, and by Mr. Macdonell, an official of the Canadian Pacific railway in Montreal. They advanced $200,000 before the election, and they increased the advance to $350,000 the next two or three months thereafter. Out of $350,000, I state here to-night that $100,000 was paid to a member of the Government of New Brunswick for the election fund for the elections of 1912, and I state here further that $97,000 of that amount is still owing by these gentlemen to the Prudential Trust Company. You now get some idea as to why the money was handled as it was, and the Minister of Railways can go back now and see why the road has not
been completed to Grand Falls and why he ought to be compelled to operate that road.
Will the hon. gentleman let me know what this has to do with running the railway, and, even if it be all true, what has this Government to do with it?
I am trying to enlighten the Minister of Railways.
I do not see where it comes in on the operation of the road.

I am trying to show the minister why this road has not been completed. The minister may say: You have not lived up to the contract, and therefore I am not bound to operate the road and if I do not operate it you are going to lose the money.

I never said so.
Mr, CARVELL: I have said so and I have shown the minister. The best evidence is that what I have said hurts him.
Oh, no.

It has all the evidence
of it.
Oh, no.

I am trying to show
my friend why the money was squandered as it was, and that as a result of the squandering of that money the road has not been completed. I know that very strong representations have been made to the minister, to Mr. Gutelius, to the Intercolonial authorities generally, to operate this road according to the contract. I know that representations have been made by the Government of New Brunswick and by the railway company; and I know that they are all truly penitent to-day for their sins, and would like at least to have the road operated, because they realize now the crime that is being practised on the province. They realize that we are liable to pay interest on about $4,000,000 for the road already completed, and that we are paying or liable to pay interest on $L,200,000; which is in the hands of the Prudential Trust Company, and which should have gone into the building of the road. They are trying to make amends, and I know they have been importuning my hon. friend the minister to operate the road according to the contract; but so far as I know he has not done so. Instead of operating the road, instead of giving the people of New Brunswick that proportion to which they are entitled, he is giving them nothing; but

if there is a loss in the operation of the road, in addition to paying the interest on the bonds and bearing other burdens, they will have to put their hands into their pockets and pay one-half of any such loss. How long is this to continue? Is it to be forever? Will my hon. friend forever be able to find some quibble and say: Your road is not yet completed. No man can ever say that a road i.s completed 'if the minister or the other party to the agreement says it is not, because building a railroad is not like binding a book or building a house, but is something which any man can say is not completed. A man anight go back a hundred times and do everything the minister wants him to do, and yet the minister might say there was some other thing that should be done. There would never be a finality. Is the minister to take that course, or will he get off his perch and be reasonable and -say that this road is completed to all intents and purposes? I want to say on behalf of the railway company, for whom I hold no brief whatever, that they have honestly endeavoured to complete the road. I believe they have, during the last six months or a year, done everything which lay in their power to get that road completed, to see a finality of it, to get the Intercolonial to take it over and operate it according to the terms of the contract. But it seems there is nothing which they -can do, nothing which the Government of New Brunswick can do, no atonement for their sins which will satisfy their lord and master the Minister of Railways. It seems to be impossible to get him to carry out his part of the agreement and to place both them and the province of New Brunswick in the position in which they ought to be placed. I do not blame my'hon. friend if lie chides his friends in the province of New Brunswick very severely. In fact in my judgment he cannot castigate them strongly enough to repay them in any degree for the sins which they have committed. He can castigate them just as severely as he chooses, but there is no reason why he should castigate innocent people while he is trying to pay back a little of the political debt he owes to his friends in the province. Every one in the province of New Brunswick says that he should 9 p.m. complete the road; but it is not our fault if the road has not been completed. The sin rests at the door of his political friends in the province of New Brunswick. Let him wreak his vengeance upon them in any way he sees fit. I.et him not wreak his vengeance 
upon the innocent man who really wants the road constructed, the man who has not the railway facilities and who has to pay interest on that debt, because the road is not constructed. I may have spoken a little plainly to-night, but that was my intention. I may have said some things to-night which the minister may think I should have left unsaid.
No.

I think, however, I
have said enough to show the minister that he, unwittingly perhaps, is wreaking his vengeance upon the wrong party. He is making every one suffer when he is perfectly justified in making his political friends suffer in any way in which he possibly can. I believe I have given the minister sufficient information to-night to justify careful investigation into the matter so far as he is concerned; to justify probing into the whole transaction in order to find out whether or not the facts I have told him to-night are borne out by the record; to justify his going into the matter to see why his friends have not carried out their part of the agreement; to see whether the fault lies with the Government of New Brunswick or with the gentlemen who are their friends, namely, the railway company. I do not know that I can say they are his friends, because I know of no connection between this Government and the railway company, excepting that I know that until about six or eight months ago the railway company could get anything they wanted in Ottawa. When things did not go right in New Brunswick they came to Ottawa and got whatever they wanted. I believe there has been a change in the relations between the department and the railway company in the last sfk or eight months.
There is another point in which my friend is to blame that this railway has not been completed, and this is a very serious one. While my friend perhaps did not want me to speak about the sins of his friends in New Brunswick, I know he will be glad to hear me discuss the other point, because it is strictly germane to the issue. I have tried to point out to my hon. friend the practical impossibility of ever making that road a financial success or of ever carrying out what it was intended it shouldbe by the promoters unless it connects with the Transcontinental somewhere at or near Grand Falls; but in order to connect with the Transcontinental at that point or at

any other place in the vicinity, that road must cross the river St. John. Unless my hon. friend wishes the road to parallel the Canadian Pacific railway running along the St. John river from Andover to Grand Falls, he must build a bridge across the river. Just where his friends intend to tap the Transcontinental, I do not know; it has been a political football for a number of years in our province about getting to Grand Falls with the Valley railway. Some of us were doubting Thomases to such an extent that we never believed that my friend intended the railway to go there at all; but of course my hon. friend's political friends always protested in the loudest and most pious manner possible that they had no other intention on earth except to go to Grand Falls. When I had the chief engineer of the railway company under cross-examination last summer, I found that they had never even surveyed a road from Andover to Grand Falls, and that they never intended to go to Grand Falls at all. They thought they might strike the Transcontinental som,e five or six miles south of Grand Falls. From the transportation standpoint, it does not make much difference where they strike the Transcontinental, so long as they get there; but from the standpoint of accomihodation and business of the people, the railway should go to the town of Grand Falls, as was promised. In order to reach Grand Falls, my hon. friend must build a bridge across the St. John river. It will be a fairly important bridge, and will cost probably two or three hundred thousand dollars; including approaches, perhaps a little more.
This Act of 1912 provided, and the minister solemnly covenanted to carry it out, for the guarantee of the bonds to the extent of $1,000,000 with which to assist the building not only of that bridge but of two others, one across the St. John at Mistake, and the other across the Kennehecasis. But the railway company came back to him and said: We can not build these bridges with an assistance of $1,000,000, and must have more money. I know not whether that be true, but they convinced the minister that they could not-
I was not here.

I know the hon. minister does not. wish me to say who was the real culprit, if I may use that word, in this transaction. But let us speak of the department; they convinced the department that they could not build the bridges with
that assistance, and I think they said that they ought to have $3,000,000. I confess I objected to that; I did object to having $3,000,000 handed over to these people for the purpose of building bridges or anything else. We had had experience with them. I say to the credit of the department, they conceded the point, and they agreed to build these bridges outright. The legislation providing for this was passed ten or eleven months ago. The minister and his department agreed to build the bridges no matter what they cost-a bridge across the St. John at Andover, a bridge across the St. John at or near Mistake, and a bridge across the Kennehecasis river. And the hon. gentleman agreed, in effect, to build these bridges at once. Oh, yes; don't deny that. There was a clause in this legislation as presented to the House providing that before the department could act they must have the consent of the Legislature of the province of New Brunswick. I pointed out to the minister at that time that the Legislature of the province of New Brunswick had then prorogued and that it would not be possible to get cohsent from them for a year, and so if they passed the legislation as it stood the effect would be to put the work off for a year. On account of my pointing this out the Bill was changed, that clause was cut out and the matter left open. So, while there was no distinct pledge either by the Government direct or through this legislation that they would build these bridges at once, still that was the real contract. For if they had put the legislation through as provided it would necessarily have caused delay of about a year and, as the result of my protest, they cut out that clause and so provided that they could go on as quickly as they liked. So, I must hold the Minister guilty of not carrying out another cpntract, solemnly made, with the people of New Brunswick.
The minister may say that this is a tremendous task. So it may be. But, no matter what may be said about the bridges on the lower part of the river, and whether the minister has an alternate scheme or not- and let him fight that out with his friends in New Brunswick-there is no reason why he should delay the building of the bridge at Andover. He ought not to have lost a day in the construction of that bridge. There are no engineering difficulties. If he will send down an engineer, that engineer ought to be able in two weeks to obtain the data necessary to draw the plans and specifications necessary for the building of that bridge. And nott only is it easy of con-

struction, it is absolutely vital to the whole undertaking. For, without that bridge as I have said, he cannot get connection with the Transcontinental, without which the whole scheme is a failure and will never carry out the objects intended and will never pay the interest on the investment.
When he answers me, I 'hope the minister will take into consideration both branches of the case that I have presented. I hope he will not try to find excuses-that is no remedy for our trouble-but will forcefully take this matter in hand, as he above all other members of the Government has power to do. We know the minister to be a forceful man. When he takes a thing into his head he usually puts it through. And we know that if he went after this matter in that way he has the power and the ability to go on with it. He will not only be able to find out where the blame lies for the condition of affairs there, but will be able to satisfy himself-and I believe will come to the conclusion-that he cannot move a moment too soon. He will find his first duty, I believe, to be to build the bridge at Andover, and the second to find out without a moment's delay where is the money obtained for the sale of these bonds nearly three years ago,-whether that money is available, and if not, why not; and if it is available then why the Government of the province of New Brunswick does not build that road to Grand Falls, make the connection with the Transcontinental and put the scheme into a position where it will not be, as the minister will tell you it is, a money-losing venture, but where it may be a boon and benefit to thousands and tens of thousands of people living in the most fertile portions of New Brunswick, and I believe one of the most fertile portions of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. FRANK COCHRANE (Minister of Railways and Canals):
speechtext:
As to the statement of the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Car-vell), I must take strong exception to his statement of facts, and indeed must give him a flat contradiction. In the first place, the difference between the two Acts is an engineering point. I make the statement on my responsibility as a minister, and after discussing this matter with people who understand the operation of railways fully as well as my hon. friend does, that the road that is being built now can be operated just as cheaply as the one proposed by the late government in the statute of 1911. That is the statement made to me by men who are ready to back up their opinion, men whose business is the operation of railways, while

the hon. gentleman himself will admit that he is not an operating man. Now, as to the operation of the road, the statute is very clear on it. The railway company, the	contractors	who	are building
this road, notified us that the road would be ready for operation between certain points on the 15th October last. On the 3rd of November, the engineers of the Intercolonial railway went over that portion of the road accompanied by representatives of the railway and representatives of the New Brunswick Government, and they had to admit that the road was not completed. We gave them a list of the parts that were not completed.
Has the minister got that list handy?
No.
I would like to see it.

They have got it. My hon. friend knows that the road was not completed, the terminals were not completed at Woodstock, his own home town. Nor were the terminals completed at Fredericton. The province of New Brunswick and the railway company wanted to enter into some kind of agreement with us under which we should complete the work, and we have undertaken to do it, giving them a service that the traffic there demands, and with the direct understanding that if there is a loss the Government of New Brunswick pays half and we pay half. He is a good man who in these stringent times carries out an agreement as I have endeavoured to carry out the provisions of this legislation. I make no bones about it; I say the road was not completed; they had to admit that it was not completed. If we carry out the letter of the law, what right has my hon. friend or the province or any one else to ask us to spend money which we are not authorized to spend? There is not a railway in the Dominion of Canada today that operates on a 60 per cent basis and furnishes rolling stock as well; yet we have entered into an agreement with the province and with this railway company to do that, and when the road is completed we will carry out our contract to the letter. As to the part of the line running to Gage-town, this we have had examined by our traffic men with a view to seeing what business there would be for the road in that section. Last Friday we came to the conclusion that we would give the people of that district a service on that portion of the line.

It may not be as good as the other, but it will give them an outlet. We have tried to meet their desires in every possible way. No money was voted for this purpose, and we had to get a Governor General's warrant in order to enable us to operate this section. As to the construction of the road, the Act does no more than give us authority to see that the road is constructed according to the specifications agreed upon by the railway company and the department. We have endeavoured to carry that out to the letter, and have made no changes which the Act does not authorize us to make.
I am sorry that I am not quite as familiar with the matter of the bridges as I should be, owing to the fact that I was not here when the Act was passed last session. I think, however, that it would he a great mistake for the province, the railway company or the people of Canada to spend millions to run the line to St. John unless the traffic proves to be much heavier than we estimate it will be. It is the intention of the Government to try to make some connection between the Transcontinental and this road. I do not know whether it is best and cheapest to make it at Grand Falls, or whether it would .be better to make it at some other point. We cannot possibly make a connection which will not get through traffic, and if we make connection with the Transcontinental at the cheapest possible point, we can get through traffic from Montreal and other points to St. John. This would not only be a shorter route of transportation than on the Intercolonial, but the resulting traffic would help to pay the cost of operation and keep the road up to a better standard.
