I think there is one thing in the statutes of 1912-and which was not in the legislation of 1911-for which we can take credit. We have the right to issue bonds on betterments, which in the case of private roads would ordinarily be charged to capital, and if the road is ever worth it we will get our money back in that way. I have consulted practical railway men, men who have been in the business for years; men who have been financing betterments and that sort of thing on such railways as the Canadian Pacific Railway- and they tell me Chat his clause in the statute, which was new to them, is worth a good deal to any road which has to be run on such a basis as we are running this one.
In the matter of the construction of the road, what the provincial Government has
not done is not a matter for me or for this Government or for this House. I have endeavoured to keep up to the limit our part of the agreement. I have endeavoured to see that we did not pay them a cent out of Dominion subsidies more than they were entitled to, and I propose to continue to do that, so far as I am able, and to see that we get a road that is constructed according to the specifications-of which, by the way, the hon. gentleman can get a copy if he wants to. The hon. gentleman started out by trying to lead the House to believe that there were no specifications, and he afterwards said that the engineer had tried to see that the specifications were lived up to. There were specifications, and there are specifications still.
I do not think that technically or in any other respect I have done anything but what is right and what is my duty. I have no right to overstep my powers and spend the people's money when I have no authority to do so, and I am not going to do it. The Act is quite plain; it says that when forty miles are completed we shall operate the line under the terms of the statute. This I intend to do and will do. The distance to Gagetown is not forty miles, yet we are going to put the line in operation. I am satisfied, from the report made by the traffic men, that operation will be at a loss, but I want to help as much as possible, and I am trying to do it by giving the people of that section one train a week. If the traffic warrants it, we will give them two trains a week. I am satisfied that we have carried out our part of the agreement to the letter of the law. We have nothing to do with the province; if they made a bad investment, the province is worth it, and we will not be put in the hole on that account. They have their share to bear, and must bear it.

I thank the hon. gentleman for the very frank statement which he has made, but I should have been pleased if he had been a little more explicit as to how be expects to connect with the Transcontinental.
That is a matter of engineering which cannot be determined at the present time.
I should have been glad if he had been more explicit m the matter of whether he intends to build the bridge at Andover, because that is the essence of the whole thing.
The railroad is not there yet.

It ought to he there. My hon. friend does not have to say more than lie wants to; I have given him the opportunity of telling us all about it, and I am pointing out the matters in respect of which he lias been hardly as explicit as he might have been. My hon. friend says that he has been advised by competent operating men that this road can be operated just as cheaply as the road we proposed. I can only say that we proposed a road which maintained a four-tenths grade, except in two places where it was necessary to exceed that to some extent. My hon. friend may have a fetish for velocity grades; I think he has. If he confined himself to velocity grades, I would not cpiarrel with him so very much, but I want to tell him that there are two places along the river St. John between Fredericton and Woodstock, a distance of 62 miles, where the railway leaves the river and climbs hills 175 feet high, and then comes back to the river again.

And you had two
pusher grades.

Not in that place. We had pusher grades, but they were necessary. I am telling my hon. friend now that pusher grades have been built in places where there was absolutely no necessity for them; they have made a one per cent grade four or five miles in length, both ways, north and south. They are not velocity grades; they are pusher grades of one per cent. Yet my hon. friend says he is advised by his traffic managers that he can operate that line just as cheaply as he could operate a road having a four-tenths grade. Well, that may be my friend's opinion and that may be the advice he is getting from his officials, but, if it is, it is something entirely new in the railway world.
My hon. friend also says it is a good man, who carries out his agreement in these hard times. Heavens, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Railways says that the Government ought to have credit because they carry out their agreement in these hard times! That is a most remarkable statement coming from the Minister of Railways, a minister with all the resources of this Dominion at his back, a member of a Government that can go out and borrow fifty or a hundred million dollars and add to the cost of the poor man's living by adding $30,000,000 more ir>
taxes, simply

by turning his hand over, and then he says the Government are entitled to a great deal of credit because they carry out that which the law makes them carry out and they will not operate this road simply because, as a matter of law, you cannot make them do it. If the minister wants to take that position he is welcome to it. I do not think his friends and followers and supporters would entirely like to sanction a position like that in many measures affecting the government of this country. He says it is a bad bargain for the Dominion and they are going to lose money. Because they are going to lose money he will not touch it until he is compelled to, and he does not believe there is a road in Canada which is operated on sixty per cent of gross earnings with the road furnishing rolling stock and equipment. Why right in New Brunswick there is the road we were discussing this afternoon, from Perth in Victoria county to Plaster Rock, which is being operated by the Canadian Pacific railway on a sixty per cent basis, the Canadian Pacific railway getting sixty per cent only of the gross earnings, furnishing rolling stock and, more than that, betterments. They are adding betterments to the amount of thousands of dollars every year, and during the ten or twelve years they have had the road have spent vast amounts of money on it. We know it is doing good business, and I have no doubt it is paying. The very best evidence that the Canadian Pacific railway is making it pay is the fact which I gave this afternoon, that when the minister first tore up the railway connection with the j?oad the Canadian Pacific railway came along and said:	Leave the track down
there and give us the business; we want the business and wish to carry it on as before. The Canadian Pacific railway does not ask for business if it does not pay. My hon. friend has a good many things to learn about railway operation. He may know something about railway finance and political railways but he has many things to learn about railway operation.
I am glad indeed to have had the perfectly frank statement we have had. P am glad the people of New Brunswick will know that the minister does not intend to operate this road excepting as the law demands and as he could almost be compelled to do by application to the court for a mandatory injunction. I only wish we had the power to go to the court and get a mandatory injunction; if so, it would be easy to find some one who would not hesitate to move, but unfortunately we

cannot get such an injunction against the Government of Canada. Only that protects him and I am glad that he takes the frank and full position he does to-night and says that he will not do it because we cannot, as a matter of law, compel him to do it.
Motion agreed to.

speakeroldname: Mr. F. B. CARVELL (Carleton, N.B.) moved:
speechtext:
For a copy of all letters, telegrams, correspondence, leases, and other documents relating to the cutting of lumber by Mr. B. F. Smith, and others from the so-called Tobique Indian reserve in the province of New Brunswick since the twelfth day of March, AD. 1914, and also of all agreements, offers and premises made either by the' said B. F. Smith or the Department of Indian Affairs, with reference to the sale or disposal of any of the said Tobique Indian reserve since the said date, or any logs or lumber cut thereon.
2. Also a statement of all lumber cut by the said B. F. Smith from the said reserve, the rates of stumpage charged, and the amounts actually paid thereon from the first day of January, 1912, down to the date hereof.
He said:	During the last general session of the House I asked a number of questions about some very curious transactions that were taking place in New Brunswick over timber being cut on Indian land. I got some information of it and finally moved for a return of all the papers and documents in connection with it. Some time in March I got a return down to the 12th day of March. The notice of motion which I have given and to which I am speaking now asks for a continuation of that return from the I2th day of March, 1914, down to the present time. I have not very much to say upon this particular question now except that I would like to get the remainder of the file in order that we may have the whole story. It is without any doubt something which should have been probed up at an earlier date and something which I am glad to say has been probed to some extent and will prob-bably be probed further. The minister has acted w'ith reasonable discretion since the matter was brought to his attention by myself in asking a question and asking for the return. The Tobique Indian Reserve is a pretty important piece of property situate near the town of Andover in Victoria county. It is divided into two parts by the Tobique river. It fronts on .the river St. John, one portion north of the Tobique river and the other south. On that portion north of the Tobique the band resides They are a very thrifty people, they have
quite a large village, a church and school; and they have made pretty fair progress towards civilization. On that part south of the Tobique, by some arrangement, the department have the right to sell the land and give title; and some time in 1913 a gentleman by the name of B. F. Smith of Carleton east longing eyes on the lumber on the reserve. He came to Ottawa and made a contract with the department by which he had the right to cut the dead and burnt timber on that portion of the reserve lying south of the Tobique river; but it was distinctly, stated in the contract that no green or partly green trees were to be cut by him. My friend will find that on page 79 of the return. It is very explicit, so explicit indeed that I hardly understand how there could be any question about it. It is as follows:
Department of Indian Affairs,
Ottawa, May 8, 1913.
Sir,-Referring to your recent interview at the department concerning the offers for the burnt timber on the Tobique reserve, south side of the river, I have to inform you that your offer of $1.25 per thousand feet, B.M., free of dues, has been accepted on the conditions that no green or partly green trees shall be cut and that sworn returns of measurement shall be furnished each season during three years allowed for its removal, by an authorized scaler, culler or surveyor, and that payments shall be made before removal of the timber from the reserve.
That was in May 1913. As soon as the logging season opened up in 1913, I think in the latter part of November or the first of December, the department received a communication by wire, signed " Tobique Indian," a telegram dated November 25, 1913, a letter dated November 29, 1913, and another letter, dated 1st of December. In all of these the department was apprised of the fact that white men were cutting green timber on the north side of the reserve. It is no secret now, because the report shows that the gentleman who signed the name of the Tobique Indian was none other than the Rev. Father Ryan, missionary, who is in charge of the Indians, the parish priest, and a gentleman who gives every attention and vigilance to the discharge of his duties that he posibly can. In addition to that, he occupies the position of a sort of inspector for these Indians and receives a small gratuity from the Government for so doing. Acting in what he considered to be his right and his duty, he notified the department of what was going on. The department sent down an inspector, an officer by the name of Mr. Bury. This gentleman acted with the very greatest energy and zeal, and certainly the depart-

ment ought to be congratulated on having in its employ a gentleman who acted as fearlessly and honourably as this gentleman did in investigating this matter. He sent in two reports; I am not going to weary the House by reading them. He sent one under date of December 12, and another under date of December 23, and in these reports he told the story' as it was, stating that he had found man after man, operator after operator, cutting green lumber open and above board in every manner, and that they had said they had been instructed by the Indian chief and that the Indian chief had said that there was a contract with Mr. Smith. This gentleman had got the right to cut dead and burnt timber on the south side of the reserve, and he started in to clean out every green tree on the north side of the reserve, which timber represented an enormous amount of money in proportion t'o the size of the reserve. The timber on the north side would be worth $16,000 or $20,000, and this gentleman started in to clean it up. On account of the action and reports of Mr. Bury this was partially stopped and then, in order to have a sacrifice of some kind, they started after the poor old Indian chief and the department gave instructions to prosecute him. The chief was prosecuted and fined- $2,000, and because he could not pay the fine he was sent to jail and remained in jail for a month. Then the demand came that something should be done with the white man who had put the chief in this position and who was really responsible for the attempt to clean up the reserve. While the return simply states what the facts are, evidently this gentleman himself had to come to Ottawa and in one of his letters he states that Mr. Hazen was looking after the matter for him. We find that a proposition comes from the^department suggesting that Mr. Smith be allowed to buy four lots on the south side of the reserve and pay a certain amount of stumpage for the lumber which has been cut on the north side. Quite a large amount of correspondence took place about the buying of these four lots. The lots, I think, were numbers 19, 21, 23 and 25. At any rate, they were four lots on the south side of the reserve. A very nice scheme was worked out and Mr. Smith was allowed to take these lots on settlement conditions, paying down the sum of $353 and agreeing to pay, in four	or
five	equal annual instalments,	a
sum amounting to somewhere between $1,100 and $1,200. He had been cutting 
the lumber and up to this time he had possibly cut. over half a million feet of green lumber on this reserve. It would never do to prosecute Mr. Smith and put him in jail, because Mr. Smith was an important gentleman. He could not be treated as the Indian was, so this scheme was worked out for him. My hon. friend knows that the settlement conditions require that a certain amount of land be cleared; that a house be built and that certain homestead duties be performed. Of course my hon. friend is thoroughly familiar with the conditions. He will find them in "Regulations for the disposal of Indian Lands," section 3, and also the penalty provided in section 4 for cutting lumber contrary to the regulations of the department. Section 3 provides that:
Settlement on the lot or lots included in any sale, is one of the conditions thereof, and shall consist of actual occupation and improvement of the land, which must commence within six months from the date of sale and be continuous for a period of three years; within which time there shall be cleared and fenced at least five acres in every one hundred acres, or in that proportion, also a dwelling-house of not less than 18 x 24 feet must be erected on the land included in any sale.
How many lots had he P

this lumber was delivered to Mr. Smith by contract on the bants of the River St. John for somewhere about $7.68 a thousand, and it would cost him from thirty to thirty-five cents to get it to Mr. Smith's mill, making the timber stand him about $8 at his mill, while that lumber last summer on the river St. John was worth $13 just as much as one dollar is worth another. Mr. Smith has made a profit of several thousand dollars on the logs, and he had the land left.
I suppose the Minister will say that this land was of no value, but he may be surprised when I tell him that Mr. Smith sold the land, after he had taken off this enormous amount of lumber, for almost as much as he paid the Department. He offered to sell it to a client of mine who came to me to know whether the title was all right and I told him it ought to be because from the information I got in Parliament this land had been sold to Mr. Smith. I wired to the Department some time in the month of January, and I got the answer back that he could not give a title for the land as it had been sold to him under settlement conditions, which conditions had not been performed. As the Minister is dealing with the property of the wards of the Government and is trustee for them, the House is entitled to know from the Minister everything that happened in connection with this transaction. In the answer given me on the 23rd of March 1 was told that this gentleman had paid $1,765 and the other amounts mentioned, in that and other answers, but eight months later I was told that he could not give a title'because he had obtained this land on settlement conditions. I cannot understand that. There may be some good explanation for this and I hope the Minister will give it to us. When the remainder of the file is brought down perhaps the matter will be made clearer than it is now. In my experience there never has been a bolder attempt made to take from the wards of the Government their right and their patrimony than was made in this case. I give the Minister of the Interior credit for acting with a good deal of alacrity when the matter was brought to his notice both by the reverend gentleman to whom I have referred and myself. After this thing was done the Minister did all he reasonably could to protect the interests of his wards with justice to all parties. I can, if the Minister wishes, give him the name of the gentleman who purchased the property from Mr. Smith and the amount he paid for it, and it is almost as much as Mr. Smith paid for it before

he took off the valuable lumber. Mr. Smith has made a large profit on it after paying the amount of money which the Minister has demanded of him for the lumber, and still he is selling the land for nearly as much as he paid for the whole thing.
While I give the Minister of the Interior credit for attempting to stop the transaction after it was brought to his attention, I cannot give the Department the same credit for allowing the matter to proceed in its initial stages. I want to say also that the Minister was not present at the time this transaction was worked off in the beginning. I do not hold the Minister responsible but l do hold his Department responsible. I hope that my hon. friend will bring down these papers; that they will make clear what now seems to be very badly muddled; that it will be a warning, and that the remainder of that reserve, whatever it may be, will be kept for the purpose for which it was intended to be kept and that the wards of the Government will not have taken from them that which at least the law intends for their protection and support.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. J. ROCHE (Minister of Interior):
speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
This matter was dealt with in the usual way departmentally, and I do not remember that it was ever brought to my attention until after the hon. gentleman had asked his respective questions which he had placed upon the order paper during the last session of Parliament. The hon. gentleman, while speaking on the previous motion, I understand spoke on behalf of his client. On this occasion, however, I understand that he is speaking in opposition to the gentleman whom he had the honour of opposing at the last general election, namely, Mr. Smith, and I do not know whether his animadversions are at all influenced by that fact. I am not saying that they are. Of course the hon. gentlemaji is quite within his rights in bringing this matter to the attention of the House.
The fact is that there was some dry timber, burned timber, ocn the reserve, on the north side and also more particularly on the south side, for the cutting of which timber tenders were asked by the department. Tenders were received from two parties, one amounting to fifty cents per thousand and the other, Mr. Smith's, amounting to $1.25.
Not his first tender.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
No. The first tender was seventy-five cents, and Mr. Smith subsequently enlarged it to a dollar and a quarter.

Shortly after that-I think it was the latter part of the month of November, or the early part of December-it was drawn to the attention of the departmental officers that trespasses were being committed on the north side of the reserve and that Chief Lockwood, the Indian in charge, had been issuing permits, not only to Indians but to white men, to cut timber on the reserve. The chief exceeded his authority in that respect, as he had no right to issue any permits. In fact, he had cut on the reserve some three hundred logs. When this complaint was brought to the attention of departmental officers by Father Ryan, Mr. Bury was sent down by the department to investigate. He sent one report in on the 12th of December and another one on the 23rd of December to the effect that wholesale cutting-to use 'his own words-had been going on by white men as well as by Indians on the reserve. While the hon. gentleman states that a vast amount of timber has been cut on the north side of the reserve-
I did not say that a vast amount had been cut on the north side; I said on the south side.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Well, on the south side, outside of the four lots which Mr. Smith was permitted to purchase. I happen to know exactly what Mr. Bury has reported as the total cut on the south side, and it amounts to 83,700 feet outside of the four lots, and 179,850 feet inside the four lots, which is far below the amount which the hon. gentleman has stated.
My hon. friend is in error in the figures he ha.s given.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I am quoting from the report which Mr. Bury sent in. He gives the names of all the parties who did the cutting. The hon. gentleman is comparing the treatment accorded the chief
10 p.m. with the treatment accorded Mr. Smith, and states that the same treatment should be accorded the latter. My hon. friend knows perfectly well that the Indian comes under the Indian Act, and that the white man does not. The chief issued permits, although unauthorised to do so; he cut some 300 logs, and, when the investigation was made by Mr. Bury, he went around and defaced the logs by cutting off the seizure marks, which was a very wrong thing for him to do, and he hindered Mr. Bury very much in connection with the investigation and report. As a matter of fact, the Indian could have
been prosecuted under the criminal code, and the penalty, not only for the trespass but for his defacement of the logs, would have been three years' imprisonment without the option of a fine. The department did not wish to take such harsh measures against the chief, and therefore they laid an information against him for having cut a hundred logs illegally. Under the Indian Act the penalty is twenty dollars for each log, or a total fine of $2,000, or, failing that, imprisonment for from one to three months. Inasmuch as the amount exceeded $20, the penalty of three months' imprisonment could have been imposed, but the minimum penalty was imposed by way of imprisonment. The chief could not pay the fine, so he was put in jail for thirty days. That penalty was imposed under section 128 of the Indian Act, which was applied to the chief because lie was the chief and was setting a bad example to the other Indians. The section reads as follows:
Every Indian of the hand, who, without the license in writing of the Superintendent General, or of some officer or person deputed by him for that purpose,
(a)	cuts, carries away or removes from land in a reserve held by another Indian under a location title or by an Indian otherwise recognized by the department as the occupant thereof any of the trees, cordwood, or part of a tree, saplings, shrubs, underwood, timber or hay thereon, or removes from such land any of the stone, soil, minerals, metals, or other valuables ; or,
(b)	cuts, carries away removes from any portion of the reserve of his band, for sale and not for the immediate use of himself and his family any trees, timber, cordwood or part of a tree, saplings, shrubs, underwood or hay thereon, or removes any of the stone, soil, minerals,' metals, or other valuables therefrom for sale, as aforesaid; or,
(c)	unless with the consent of the hand and the approval of the Superintendent General, cuts or uses any pine or large timber for any purpose other than for building on his own location or farm; shall incur the penalties provided in the last preceding section in respect to Indians of other bands and other persons.
The penalty referred to in the next preceding section is:
For every tree he cuts, carries away or removes, a penalty of twenty dollars.
That was the penalty imposed on the chief. It was impossible to impose the Indian Act on the white man. If we were to utilize the Indian Act to every trespasser every person who has a license and who trespasses, whether wittingly or unwittingly, I think we would .have the treasury replenished by many millions of dollars. It is a very common thing for a licensee to go beyond the land for which he holds a

Had Mr. Smith the
right to cut the lumber?	-

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
No, he was fined for cutting the timber outside his lease from the Crown to the amount of treble dues, and in

lieu of these treble dues, he was allowed to purchase these four lots at an average price * of about $4 an acre, as against $1 an acre which had been charged for many years before.
But has he the right to cut the lumber on these lots?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I have not before me the return the hon. gentleman has quoted. I will bring down the remainder of the papers he has moved for. There is no objection to bringing them down; there is nothing whatever to hide, and certainly nothing that I am conversant with that we need be ashamed of. As the hon. gentleman says, when the matter was brought to my attention, I made inquiries, and Mr. Smith was instructed that he must live up to his contract. I do not know whether he has applied for the patents or not, but most assuredly he has not received them, and settlement conditions must -be complied with, and compliance with them proven, before patent will issue. I do not know that there is anything I can add. The hon. gentleman will see that we cannot treat the white man exactly as the Indian is treated under'the Indian Act. As I have said, it is not uncommon for a lumberman to cut in trespass and, in some cases, where it has been done by inadvertence, only single dues are charged. It is common to charge double dues; but in the case of Mr. Smith he was charged treble dues. For what he had cut on the north side he paid in cash, and outside the lots he bought on the south side he paid treble fees, while the lots he was allowed to purchase at four times the price at which the former Government sold similar lands on the same reserve.

I thought I threw
enough bouquets at the minister to cause him to answer in a little different spirit. I tried to tell him that in my judgment he at least had tried to act fairly in the matter, and I thought that the department also had tried to protect the interests of the Indians. He is in error, however, in some of the statements he has made-innocently in error, of course. When he says that the former Government sold these lands at $1 an acre, that, I presume, is true. I never had anything to do with purchasing such lands nor do I know of a case of a hundred acres being sold; but if he says that the price charged was $1 an acre, no doubt that is true. But there are lots of land and other lots of land; some are worth $100 and some are worth $500 or $1,000. I can 13	-
tell him that any lands sold by the late Government on the old Tobique Indian Reserve were burned over and practically useless. But I know a man who tried to get these very lots, which were timbered and desirable.
My hon. friend will find that a company known as the Perth Lumber Company made a contract with the Government to cut this burnt lumber-a fire took place some four or five years ago-which Mr. Smith had contracted to cut. They assigned their contracts to a gentleman by the name of Wentworth, of Boston, who was losing a large amount of money through his contracts with the Perth Lumber Company. I went to the department to see if it was possible to make some arrangement by which first the Perth company and latterly Mr. Wentworth could cut enough green timber to finish the operation. That was absolutely refused, it being contended that these four or. five lots of land were the only lots south of the Tobique river upon which there was any lumber. My hon. friend will find that in the days of the old Government and under the present regime the Department of the Interior never offered to sell these lots of land at $1 an acre. Had it been known that these special lots of land were available at $1 an acre, not one but a dozen or two dozen men would have been delighted to buy them. I do not know the conditions of that notice of sale, because, unfortunately, it is not in the return which I have received, but I have no doubt at all that there was some reservation; there was something which prevented the" ordinary man from knowing that these four or five lots of land were on sale.
The minister is also in error in saying that 179,850 feet of spruce and 95,330 feet of hemlock was practically all the lumber cut inside the four lots.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: By Mr. Smith.

By Mr. Smith. In that respect my hon. friend is in error, and I can prove it by referring to this file. My hon. friend will find, according to the sate-ment made by Mr. Bury in his report of December 23, 1913, that at that time Mr. Smith was only in the initial stages of the process of cutting. Up to that time it is true that he had cut only 265,000 feet of lumber, but he went on and on; my hon. friend will find that telegram after telegram was sent in regard to the matter. The amount of lumber cut by Smith on this land and on the adjoining lot was nearer 750,000 feet than 265,000 feet. It is



true that down to December 23, 265,000 feet is an approximate estimate of the amount of lumber cut, but Smith did not stop; he went on and, I presume, finished the job. I say this not for the purpose of finding fault, hut in order to point out the real facts of the matter. According to this Mr. Craig, the land was worth only the amount of money paid. I tell the minister that at the end of the year 1914 the amount of lumber cut was nearly three-quarters of a million feet, and that these four lots have been and could be sold to-day-part of the purchase money has already been paid, although I suppose it will now have to be repaid-for almost as much as Mr. Smith paid for them. My hon. friend will find in the report of Mr. Bury, dated December 23, 1913, this paragraph:
Practically the whole of the growing merchantable timber on the Indian lands on the south side of the Tobique river has been cut, there being left about 1,000 trees, or approximately 60,000 feet board measure left standing on lot 25.
According to the report sent to the department by Mr. Craig, the lumber was all cut on De .ember 23, excepting 6,000 feet. Half a million feet has been cut since then, and' Mr. Smith can still turn round and sell the property for nearly as much as he paid for it. That will give you some idea of the value of the reports my hon. friend is getting. That will give you some idea of the credence with which my hon. friend can receive the evidence given him by this Mr. Craig. At the time when Craig said there were net more than 60,000 feet of lumber there, worth, according to his estimate, not more than $200, there was on the land lumber upon which a profit was made of more than $2,000, and the lot was subsequently sold for $1,500. That will give you some idea of the absolute worthlessness of the evidence upon which my hon. friend has been basing his arguments to-night. I am finding no fault with my hon. friend; I am finding no fault with Mr. Bury. Mr. Bury, in the first report which he made to the department, criticised the whole transaction in the severest possible terms. He went so far as to recommend that the contract with Mr. Smith be cancelled. Here is the report which Mr. Bury made on December 12, 1913:
I beg to confirm my wire to you as follows:
* Wholesale cutting of green timber by white men and Indians has been going on, sanctioned by Chief Lockwood. Am making thorough seizure. Chief difles seizure by removing marks from logs. Suggest suspending him from office pending completion of investigation. Letter following.'

Mr. P. B. Smith, licensee for most of the timber on south side, has several men cutting green logs on the north side, ail of whom claim that Lockwood himself gave them verbal permission to cut over 170 logs for Mr. Smith, and I have already seized a total of over 500 logs (green) cut on north side, in addition to several cords of green maple and birch cut by white men also.
I expect to seize the same number of green logs cut on the south side.
Mr. Smith has violated' the terms of his license, and I would suggest you instruct me to order all cutting to cease pending presentation of report.
This refers to Mr. Smith's operations under his three-year lease.
Chief Lockwood has received moneys from time to time from various parties in return for allowing them to operate. None of said moneys have been surrendered to agent Waite.
The chief moreover has chopped off my seizure mark on his logs, and practically defies me in the execution of my duties.
I intend making a thorough clean-up of all the illegal lumber operations both on the north and south sides of the reserve, and am of opinion that this will have a very desirable effect in preventing a recurrence of trespass.
I am also scaling all logs and wood I seize so that action for collection of dues can be commenced immediately upon my return.
'In this connection I beg leave to suggest that all these green logs be confiscated outright and sold by public auction, thus providing more valuable returns, and also establishing beyond cavil that trespassing will no longer be tolerated.
And the minister says, after receiving a report like that from a responsible officer: Oh, well, we know that these lumbermen committed trespass; we know that they cut from other people's lands. As a rule, my hon. friend says, we charge them double stumpage and sometimes single stumpage, but in this case we were unusually severe, imposing upon them the full penalty of the law. We made Smith pay treble stumpage. Could Smith have paid treble on one-tenth of what he actually cut, in the face of Mr. Bury's report.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Does that official say that the amount quoted was only one-tenth of the amount cut?

No, I say so. My hon. friend made Smith pay stumpage only on the logs that were cut when Bury was there. That was back in December, and they did not commence until the 3rd or 4th of December. Smith went on cutting logs practically all winter and really paid no stumpage on the lumber cut in December. There is where the whole trouble comes in. I did not want to go into this part of the matter, but my hon. friend attempts to excuse the transaction, and I have thought it necessary to give him a few of the

Hon. R. LEMIEUX (Rouville) (Translation) moved the following resolution:
That, In the opinion of this House, stricter measures should be taken for the carrying out of the Berne convention relative to copyright.
He said: Mr. Speaker, considering that this question concerns specially the province of Quebec, since publications in the French language are those now dealt with, I wish to address the House in French, as briefly as possible, as regards what is going on in this connection in some of our large cities in the province of Quebec.
I much regret the absence just now of the Hon. Minister of Agriculture; but I may inform the Right Hon. Prime Minister that on meeting the Hon. Mr. Burrell before recess, it was arranged between us that I should move the resolution this evening, he promising to read the report of my speech in "Hansard" and. to do his best to remedy the state of things complained of.
The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Car-veil) informed the House a moment ago of the thefts and plunder of which the New Brunswick Indians are the victims. I wish to draw the attention of the House to the thefts and plunder which other whites are guilty of at the expense of writers in the French language, whose works are sold and republished, more particularly in the province of Quebec.
As you are aware, Sir, protection for copyrights is Secured under the Berne convention. For some time there were doubts entertained as to the possibility of enforcement I think in Canada of the rules laid down by the aforesaid convention; but through the exertions of Sir John Thompson, at one time Prime Minister of the Dominion, all uncertainty in this respect has disappeared.

Following on a prolonged campaign carried on by the writers concerned, through the press in France and Canada, Mr. Jules Mary, under instructions from the "Soeiete des Gens de Lettres," of Paris, entered action in the latter part of 1905, in the Superior Court of Montreal, in the form of a test case, against a counterfeiter of that city (B. Hubert). On March 23, 1906, the Hon. Mr. Justice Fortin, before whon^the case had been heard, condemned the Montreal counterfeiter, holding that the Imperial statutes (49-50 Viet., cap. 33, sect. 9) did extend to Canada the effects of the rulings of the Berne convention which secure to writers in countries forming part of the Union protection for their rights within the territories covered by the international union, to which Great Britain has assented for herself and her colonies. On April 28 of the same year, the court of Appeal, sitting in Montreal, unanimously confirmed the aforesaid ruling of the Hon. Mr. Justice Fortin and set down the law In that respect. The pleadings will be found in the "Revue Canadienne," 1906, vol. 1, pp 252 and 535; the rulings of the courts, in the "Quebec Official Law Reports," Superior Court, vol. xxix 1906, p 334 and following; and, the same, Court of King's Bench, vol. xv., 1903, page 381 and following.
The judgment rendered in that test case of Jules Mary vs. B. Hubert had the effect of securing for some time in Canada the production of copyrights held by foreign writers. But counterfeiters were not to be deterred for any length of time, and French authors were once more constrained to apply to the courts to vindicate their rights protected in Canada under the Berne convention.
In matters of copyright claims having to do with theatricals, our civil courts lay down the following requirements which are to be observed by the French and Belgian plaintiff:
(1)	He shall find out the name of the author of this or that production advertised and given under a false description or under a false signature, or under no signature whatever;
(2)	He shall authenticate that production thus falsely represented and show that it is his property;
(3)	He shall retain the services of a Canadian lawyer;
(4)	He shall file with the Canadian courts the original text of his work and the certificate of its formal registration in its country of origin ;
(5)	He shall also file a solemn declaration duly certified in France or in Belgium, according to the case;
(6)	He shall furnish a security bound 'judi-catum solvi ';

(7)	(In the case of an editor, heir, assign or assignee) He shall, moreover, file all deeds of transfer, duly authenticated, showing that he is the rightful owner of the work.
Then the author's case is put on the list to be hoard when its turn comes at some indefinite lime.
Now it is a matter of experience that most counterfeiters form partnerships which are practically insolvent, which are likely to shift or dissolve at any moment; they are up to all the tricks which may be resorted to without technically breaking the law. So that, once posted, the French and Belgian author, whose works have been con-terfeited in Canada, hesitates, and rightly so, to comply with all such requirements of our procedure, and to run the risks of a lawsuit with possibly no other satisfaction as regards himself than the paying of a heavy bill of costs. The practical result is that Canadian counterfeiters are allowed to go scot-free.
The Berlin conference of November 13, 1908, which revised the rules laid down by the Berne convention of September 9, 1886, provided more efficient means of protection available to authors in countries belonging to the Union. But Canada, not having as yet given its assent to the rulings of the Berlin conference; authors in unionist countries whose works are counterfeited in Canada are not entitled to claim more than the protection afforded by the Berne convention, which in the absence of proper means of enforcement, is not of much more avail than a mere " scrap of paper."
' The British organic law of December 16, 1911 (applied along the lines of the Berlin Act of 1908), is already in force in most of the colonies and' possessions, save Canada and the South African Union.' ("Le Droit d'Auteur ", monthly organ of international Bureau of the Union for the protection of literary and artistic works. Berne, January 15, 1914, page 2, column 3).
I may state in passing that, on April 26, 1911, the Hon. 8. Fisher, then Minister of Agriculture, introduced in the House of Commons a Bill (No. 184) amending and revising former legislation of the Dominion Parliament relating to copyright, and framing further Canadian legislation after the Imperial modernized statute (1 and 2 Geo. V., cap. 46, 1911), which, in April, 1911, had not yet been put through the British Parliament. That Bill, introduced by the Hon. Mr. Fisher, did not imply our assent to the Berlin Act, but prepared the way for such assent, with certain reservations deemed necessary for the holding in check of competition on the part of the United States.
(See speeches of the Hon. S. Fisher, "Hansard," April 26 and May 12, 1911).
The Fisher Bill was not then passed. A general election was forthcoming in September, 1911, and the result was a change of Government in the Dominion. The Borden Administration has not in the meantime dealt with the question. Matters have remained in their former state, and foreign writers using the French language are still bound to apply to the courts for the enforcement of the imperial statute and the Berne convention.
" Unfortunately, difficulties and the cost of litigation are such as to render that protection more or less delusive. Copyrights are constantly infringed upon in Canada, in spite of the efforts of many prominent men who consider rights and equity as of greater account than prejudices or the egotistic interests of a few men."
That view, which reflects to some extent on Canada, is expressed by Mr. Leon Poin-sard, deputy head of the international offices for the protection of trade marks and copyrights at Berne (" La propriety arfisti-que et litteraire," par Leon Poinsard, p. 53; Paris, librairie generate de droit et jurisprudence, 1910).
In fact, any copyright claims in connection with theatrical productions due to other foreign writers, are enforced in Canada, under the provisions of the imperial statute 3 and 4, Wm. IV., cap. 15, sec. 2. That Act merely provides for a pecuniary fine recoverable from any one who, without the owner's authorization, produces a theatrical work. It enables the author at whose prejudice this is done, to claim either the profits secured through the illegal performance of his work, either an estimate of the loss incurred, or a statutory fine of not less than forty shillings for each unauthorized performance. It is almost impossible to get at the exact amount of profits secured; it is difficult as well to show what losses have been sustained. The simplest thing to do is to claim the statutory fine. That fine is recoverable after, going through the regular process of law. The summary procedure, by brief of injunction, to forestall the representation of a work, is not as a rule of any use in practice, and for several reasons. In the first place, programmes of theatres are changed from week to week, and in some instances several times a week, and the various attractions are usually advertised only a few days ahead. Now, according as the ease may be, the author, or his heir, or assign, or the editor who has

purchased his rights, will be expected to apply in his own name to the Canadian courts and establish his claim to the property of such or such a work. 'The " Societe des auteurs et compositeurs dramatiques " of Paris, alone has more than 50,000 works on its list. French and Belgian authors are numbered by the thousand. Several of them live in the country while others are travelling. It is utterly impossible to reach them in time to secure from them the requisite information in regard to a specific case and to transmit that information to their representatives in Canada. Besides, in a great many cases of assignment, proof of that transfer will also be required. Then, those who are acting for the " Societe des auteurs " must be posted as to the actual rights held by the owner of the work the performance of which it is the object to prevent, and must secure authority from the holder of such rights before advising the author or his assignee to fulfil the requirements laid down by Canadian courts and to furnish the required security (viz., as a rule $500 for costs and $500 for possible damages) and indeed, to run the risk of being called upon to pay heavy costs, should the counterfeiter disappear-for only insolvent impresarios or theatre managers dare infringe the law with whose provisions they are quite familiar.
The Canadian counterfeiter is therefore perfectly aware to-day that the foreign author must prove his case to the satisfaction of the Canadian law courts, and such an undertaking is not of a tempting nature. So that the first comer, however insolvent he may be, is free to lay hands on the work of a French or Belgian author, make changes to suit himself, and utilize it for performances entirely for his benefit. Our theatre season generally covers ten months or forty weeks. A company which has resolved not to pay any fees for copyright advertises every week a new French or Belgian production, makes the alterations it sees fit and gives no heed to threats of the law. To adequately protect themselves, the authors concerned would have to institute against that faithless company forty law-suits for as many plays illegally produced during those forty weeks in a single theatre, and to furnish security for as many times $500 or $1,000. The company which is thus making money out of foreign works is aware that previous to judgment being rendered, the season will be over, it will

have had time to dissolve and to re-organize itself under a new business name, owing to the delays inherent to our civil court proceedings.
I may point out here a few instances of >
such delays the effect of which has been to cause the recourse granted by our laws to actually inflict losses on the authors concerned.
(1)	The "Parisiana" theatre, of Montreal, after being formally prohibited from doing so, produced during the week beginning May 19, 1910, under the assumed title " Sherlock Holmes," and without any indication of authorship, a one-act comedy really entitled " En lisant Sherlock Holmes," and whose author, Mr. R. Berton, by the way, is at present with the French army in front of Rheims. The representatives at the "Societe des auteurs " made inquiries, and they brought to light both the name of the author and the original title of the play, which was being reproduced under false colours. They applied to Paris for the necessary documents to enable them to enter action, and these, duly authenticated and certified, were duly transmitted to them through the British consulate at Paris. The requisite security was furnished and an action entered on June 27, 1910, in the Montreal Superior Court. Judgment in favour of the author was rendered on December 17, 1912. Now, at that date, the " Parisiana " had ceased to exist and its owners were out of
sight	Apart f: om the expense
incurred on account of researches and the forwarding of documents, the author had to meet costs to the amount of about $100.
(2)	The Aborn Opera Company, of New York, produced at the " Princess " theatre in Montreal, during the week beginning on November .18, 1912, then at Toronto, during the week beginning on November 25, 1912, the play entitled " Cloches ue Crrneviue " (Chimes of Normandy). The Aborn Company having refused to settle with the author's assignees found it impossible to secure a brief of injunction for „ue following reasons which recur in a great many cases:
Editor Choudens, of Paris, had acquired full property rights in connection with the Chimes of Normandy, and had in turn transferred to the firm of James Williams & Co., of London, the right to produce that musical work throughout Great Britain and the Colonies. To secure a brief of injunction, papers proving the successive transfers were required. These papers reached here after a rather lengthy exchange of correspondence between

London and Paris, and made possible the entering of an action against the Aborn company. Judgment by default was rendered against the Aborn company on October 11, 1913. But the latter had a long time previously crossed the boundary, and they have not in the meantime revisited Canada. All the costs connected with this lawsuit had to be met by the representatives, of the author.
(3)	The " Liberty " theatre, of Montreal, though notified several months ahead, produced without authority, under assumed titles and without indication of authorship, from December 16, 1912, to February 13, 1913 (that is during a period of eight weeKs), fourteen one-act comedies of which editor Joubert, of Paris, had secured the ownership. That editor, owning a number of short plays especially well adapted to moving picture shows, is shamefully robbed in the province of v^uebec. He resolved to put a stop to such plundering by suing one of the counterfeiters, the " Liberty " theatre.
As that small theatre did not go to the expense of printing a programme, the representatives in Canada of editor Joubert had to get photographs taken of the posters outside the entrance, and to send a stenographer to report extracts of the dialogue, so as to enable a comparison of it with the author's text, and thus show proof of the counterfeiting. They had also to secure in Paris authenticated copies of all transfers and other documents relative to these fourteen plays, etc. Suit against the Liberty theatre was entered on June 15, 1913, in the Superior Court in Montreal. Sixteen months later, on November 21, 1914, judgment was rendered against editor Joubert, though at the same time acknowledging that the Berne convention affords -protection in Canada to French authors and editors. But the judge presiding ruled that it was the " Societe des auteurs, compositeurs et editeurs de mus-ique," known as the " Petite societe," which should have initiated the proceedings against the " Liberty " theatre, and not editor Joubert.
The above ruling upsets the whole procedure previously established as regards French authors who have rights to vindicate in the Canadian courts, and is in direct contradiction to the jurisprudence of the last eight years, that is, ever since the Berne convention has been assented to by the Canadian law-courts.
The case was at once taken to appeal. But the French editor concerned, besides
having to settle the cost incurred for the making of the voluminous records required in the court below, may still have to disburse $1,500 of further costs and fees, even should the Court of Appeal decide in his favour, as he will not be in a position to recoup himself on an insolvent defendant.
On another occasion we find a troop of amateurs giving performances for the benefit of some one or other. Amateurs and beneficiary are at one in refusing to indemnify the author, and the representatives of the latter are sent from the one to the other. An action was entered in one instance against amateurs giving performances without previously making arrangements with the author. Judgment was rendered for $15 and costs in favour of the author and he had to wait a whole year for his money.
Apart from itinerant or occasional companies which shamefully delve into the works of French and Belgian authors, there exists to-day, in Montreal, as well as in other localities of the province of Quebec, over ten theatres which have recourse to counterfeiting and dispense paying any royalties to authors, with full knowledge of the law. And in spite of it all, nothing can be done.
Itinerant or occasional troops give no security; they disband or cross the frontier before any process of law can be taken against them. The author wronged in that way has no possible'recourse against the owner of the hall or theatre where these itinerant companies have given their illegal performances, though the owner of the theatre often shares in the profits secured by means of these unlawful performances. The English jurisprudence exonerates the theatre owner. (Lyon vs. Knowles. See " Copinger's Law of Copyright," 4th Edition, by Easton, 1904, page 292).
As regards stock companies, which occupy permanently a theatre, the " Theatre des Nouveautes " affords us an instance of that. The " Nouveautes " theatre has been producing for the last ten months, in the heart of Montreal, French and Belgian plays. Its managers have never heeded the numerous summonses which have been served on them on behalf of injured authors; while the latter are unable to institute proceedings for this very Teason that the managers of the said theatre have not registered in the Tutelles' office, that " they are doing business under the name of ' Theatre des Nouveautes,' " in other words they have not conformed to the law which requires owners

or managers of places of entertainment to register their legal designation. The managers of this popular resort remain, from the legal point of view unknown entities.
The merchant is free to deliver or refuse to deliver goods to an insolvent patrdn acting under his own name or under that of a company. But the writer, though technically allowed, under the law, to permit or interdict the production of his work, has no means of protecting himself. He can claim compensation only when all security [DOT]for the payment of such compensation has been put out of his reach. And should he make up his mind to protest against the thefts of which he is the victim in Canada, he is -met by the exacting requirements of our civil procedure and is bound to secure numerous legal documents in France and in Belgium, which, unless they are absolutely without a flaw, are liable to be rejected. Then he must furnish security, put up one hundred dollars in the hope of getting one dollar back. For, those who prey on the author's means of living are in every case insolvents or people who cannot be reached under the law. And that seems to warrant the harsh expressions [DOT] which Mr. Leon Poinsard made use of referring to Canada's attitude on this question, in a work which deals authoritatively with the matter.
Writers in the French language who are of French, Belgian or Swiss nationality, are mainly the victims of that state of things which, moreover, stifles the growth of a French-Canadian literature. In fact, the future of French-Canadian writers is so well linked to that of their fellow-workers across the Atlantic, that within the last two years the Societe des Auteurs, of Paris, admits Canadian authors to its membership and looks after their interests. During the theatre season of 1913-14, a total amount of about $2,000, as may be vouched for and certified to by the Bank of Hoche-laga, was paid over to French-Canadian authors, through the intervention of representatives of the society.
By the way, I may inform the House that the aforesaid society has effected a kind of merger, whereby all Frenchspeaking writers have assigned their rights to it, the latter in return undertaking to safeguard such rights.
Authors in France protested in various ways against the abnormal situation in which they were left in Canada. Their representatives on several occasions approached the Dominion authorities in order to secure some redress. The Royal

Society of Canada, at its meeting of May, 1913, passed a resolution urging the Dominion Government to model Canadian legislation after more effective and up-to-date enactments adopted elsewhere. The society reiterated that resolution at its meeting of May, 1914. But matters are left in the same state, opposition to any improvement in our copyright legislation centering apparently in the great body of Ontario editors and publishers, who are not in the least anxious that copyrights held by foreigners be protected here to the same extent as they are elsewhere.
The hon. Minister of Justice, whom I am glad to see at his seat, will no doubt inquire what remedy or what means I would suggest to bring about an improvement. I am prepared to offer some suggestions.
In the first place, if possible, measures should be taken requiring that organizers of entertainments should register at once with the authorities and secure a license, which, if need be, should guarantee any loss resulting from any action of theirs. Of even greater importance would be the providing of foreign writers with a summary process of law m the form of a penalty or of imprisonment for infringement of author's rights. A sanction of that kind is to be found in the legislation of most civilized countries, especially England (1 and 2 Geo. V, chapter 46, section 11); of most self-governing colonies, especially New Zealand (Act of November 22, 1913, section 15); in that of France (Penal Code, section 428429), without in any way depriving authors of their recourse under section 1362 of the Civil Code; even in that of the United States, though they stand aloof from international unions (United States statutes at large, chapter 320, " An Act to amend and consolidate the Acts respecting copyright," March 4, 1914, sections 28 and 39); etc., etc.
At the session of 1909, Sir Allan Ayles-worth, then Minister of Justice, introduced in the House of Commons a Bill (No. 148) amending the Criminal Code. That Bill comprised among others a clause providing a penalty for counterfeiting of musical and dramatic productions. After discussion that clause was modified as follows:
Whosoever, after a dramatic work has been registered, performs or produces in public, or in some way causes to be performed, or assists in the performance or production in public, in whole or in part, of such dramatic work, without the consent of the owner, is (unless he shows that he has done so innocently) guilty of a misdemeanour and liable, on summary conviction, to a fine of one hundred to five hun-

dred dollars, or to imprisonment for a period of thirty days, or to both cumulatively, at the discretion of the court, and on the second or any further conviction to imprisonment for a period of six months with or without hard labour.
The Aylesworth Bill, with that clause inserted, was passed by the House of Commons on May 15, 1909 (see "Hansard" for
1909, vol. Ill, page

; vol, IV, page

The Senate, on May 18, 1909, also passed the Aylesworth Bill, but after striking out a few clauses, especially the proposed section 508b providing protection for dramatic
works (see Senate Debates, 1909, page

).
I trust the hon. Minister of Justice will read once more the discussion which took place in this House in 1909, in regard to copyrights and to the penalty suggested by Sir Allan Aylesworth, for infringement of such rights. And I shall leave to him to say whether the time is not ripe for the passing of such a clause by this Parliament.
The facts alleged by me show that the Berne convention as it is, and with the slow procedure provided for its enforcement in Canada, or at any rate in the province of Quebec, is practically of no use in helping authors who have been wronged to secure redress from the courts of law. The hon. gentleman has been on the bench long enough to know to what extent people in Quebec are fond of litigation, and should one of the litigants be in bad faith, he may drag the matter on indefinitely, in spite of the earne'stness of the other party and of the presiding judge.
I have pointed out instances in which French writers who had been wronged found it impossible to secure compensation for the enforcement of the penalty provided by the Berne convention. Would it not be possible, then, to amend our criminal code in the sense suggested by Sir Allan Aylesworth, and to have that amendment passed by the Senate?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I believe we would need your help for that purpose.

I may be of some help to my hon. friend.
In closing my remarks, I wish to express my regret for having addressed the House at such length. But this is a question with which the honour of the nation and its reputation for honesty in literary matters are deeply concerned. That is what induces me to appeal to the Minister of Justice, and to request that he find a remedy for the evils which afflict specially French authors in this country.
I do not intend saying anything in reference to writers in the English tongue;
others who are better qualified than myself, no doubt, will take an interest in them. I repeat it, I am anxious to secure protection for the rights of those who in old France have produced masterpieces, which we are fond of reading and re-reading, or seeing performed on the stage. However, it is only fair that such a result should not be secured through an enfripgement of the most elementary principles of equity and honour.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The question of copyright is one that comes primarily to be dealt with rather by my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Burrell) as forming part of the matters that are allotted to that particular department of the Government.

I do not know that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Doherty) was present when I opened my remarks, but I stated that before six o'clock I had met the Minister of Agriculture and that he had begged me to go on, because, although he had to leave, he said " I will read your remarks in "Hansard" and deal with this matter as soon as I come back." But I am pleased to see my hon. friend (Mr Doherty) in his seat, because he can deal with this matter in the way I mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In making the observation I did I had no intention of addressing any reproach to the hon. gentleman.
I only made that observation to point out that I did not come here this evening myself anticipating that I would have the pleasure of listening to my hon. friend upon this subject and still less prepared to undertake any full discussion of the very important matter that he has dealt with. I did not have the advantage either of hearing all that the hon. gentleman has said, but if I correctly followed him, the gist of the complaint seems to be that the civil recourse of parties complaining of a violation of their rights as authors of "dramatic productions is inadequate; and furthermore, that the inadequacies would seem to result from the fact that as a rule the persons guilty of such unlawful reproduction are persons financially irresponsible as against whom it would be impossible to execute any judgment. That seemed to be one of the causes which gave rise to the inefficiency, or ineffectiveness, of the law; and the other resulted from the undue delays which occurred in the enforcement of the civil right. If I followed the hon. gentleman correctly, he does not

complain of the insufficiency of our law as it stands as recognizing the existence' of the right, but he complains simply that we have no effective sanction.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: So long as one keeps to the civil recourse, the recourse that seeks an indemnification for loss caused, there is not any method by which we can make insolvent violators of the law solvent. In so far as he points to the very regrettable consequences of the delays that occur in the procedure in connection with such civil actions, it seems to me that is something for which provincial legislation rather than any legislation of this Parliament should be responsible. I do not mean to say that perhaps it is not conceivable that we may have authority to eract some special disposition in regard to procedure in relation to the violation of copyright, but as I understand it, the procedure in cases of that kind, as in all civil cases, is at the present time governed by provincial laws, and delays in that procedure, if they be attributable to a defect in any law, would be attributable to the defects in the laws of the provinces concerned. It is undoubtedly a very regrettable thing that it should be found that, for the violation of a right which our law recognizes, that law does not at the same time provide an adequate remedy. The hon. gentleman referred to cases, where Canadian authors had succeeded under the French law in obtaining compensation for such violation of their rights.

No, I said that we ought to at least reciprocate with the French,' that the French-Canadian authors had the benefit in France of a fund which existed for the protection of their works. It operates automatically. If a man writes an article in a review he belongs to the bociete des Auteurs. If the article is reproduced in another country, the society is represented by somebody, and the party reproducing that article will have to pay a certain amount. French-Canadian authors enjoy that protection in France, but what I said was that while they had benefited from the organization for the payment of authors in Europe, in our own country French authors are being pillaged. When the victims seek redress before the courts, by the articles of the Berne Convention, they are discouraged by delays.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not know that I quite follow the hon. gentleman. I did understand that the hon. gentleman re-
ferred to some successful proceeding which had resulted in indemnity being obtained by our authors for violations occurring in France, and to urge that we should provide some similar method. If I understand correctly now, it is not the benefit which he receives as the result of any law which confers any legal right, but the result of the operation of some association which provides a fund.
A benefit fund.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is something that I do not suppose we could provide for. It is no doubt, however, a most regrettable condition of affairs if, in this country, by violations of the law of this country, persons living outside of the country suffer and if for such violations they are without adequate remedy. My hon. friend has pointed out certain grievances which are grievances shared by all persons who have recourse to the courts to enforce their rights. He points out that a foreign author would have to give security for the costs that should be incurred. If he is bound to do so, he is so bound in the province of Quebec under a provision of the law of Quebec, which I think is usually looked upon as a wise provision, that where a stranger comes into the province seeking to invoke the law against a resident, the latter should be protected to the extent of some provision being made to secure him in the event of his successfully defending himself in the action instituted against him. I do not quite grasp that that is in any particular way a grievance on the part of those who seek to enforce the particular right that may belong to a dramatic author. As regards delays, of course, in that respect dramatic authors suffer in common with the public in general, and suffer in common with our own citizens. What means may be found to expedite the civil procedure is perhaps more properly for the consideration of those who are charged with legislation as regards the procedure and administration of justice in the different provinces. I do not desire to express any absolute opinion on this subject, but it seems to me that there is a remedy to which the hon. gentleman did not refer, but which, under the law of the provinces, would be available to the authors concerned, and that would be an effective remedy in so far as it might operate as a prevention rather than a cure of the wrong that may be done. I have some difficulty in seeing why the recourse by injunction is not open to the author who is in a position to establish that any person is about to produce a work which he claims is his own,

and in which he claims to be protected by the copyright law. It seems to me that that right ought to be available and ought to operate to obviate some of the things of which the hon. gentleman spoke in discussing the position of these foreign authors, and I think it is a remedy of which they might avail themselves.
I am not disposed to quarrel with the proposition that it might be desirable that a means should be taken which womd reach persons who might be, from the point of view of civil responsibility, not in a position to comply with any judgment that may be rendered against them. From that point of view there is a great deal to be said in support of the suggestion of the hon. member (Mr. Lemieux), that this might be a proper matter to be dealt with by the criminal law. The Bill to which the hon. gentleman refers, I think passed this House without being opposed, but was rejected by the Senate. Of course, the Senate must be assumed to have good reasons to refuse to pass measures that this House adopts. At all events since the time to which the hon. member refers the Senate seems to have persisted with a good deal of consistency in the assertion of its right to annul what the wisdom of this House has decreed. We on this side of the House perhaps do not feel the same absolute confidence in being able to control the operations of that august body as do gentlemen on the other side of the House.

That shows
the independence of the Senate; it was in 1909 that they refused to pass the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I quite understand that, but I am only pointing out that they are obdurate in the determination to place themselves above what may be decreed by the wisdom of this House and that some people have thought that possibly the influence that existed at that time from this side of the House over the Senate was greater than it might be at present. If that be true, we would now have less hope of being able to convert them from their error, than had those who sat on these benches at that time. I quite recognize that the position of these authors is one which calls for careful consideration on our part, and the question as to whether or not an amendment to the criminal law such as is suggested might prove of aid to the protection of their rights is certainly one which deserves to be considered. I shall have pleasure in complying with the suggestion of the hon.
gentleman (Mr. Lemieux) to read the debates of 1909, and I shall have pleasure also in endeavouring to ascertain what reason, if any, the hon. gentlemen in the upper House set forth as justifying their action.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I regret that the Minister of Agriculture is prevented through indisposition from attending the House this afternoon. In addition to what the Minister of Justice has said, I may say that I know that the Minister of Agriculture has had the whole question of copyright under consideration during the past two years, and that representations, not so much with regard to procedure as to the substance of the law itself, and in connection with the Berlin convention, have been made to him. If I am not mistaken, negotiations have gone on from time to time, with a view to adhering, if possible, to the Berlin convention, but under such conditions as to safeguard Canadian interests, which might otherwise suffer materially, but which we would not desire to sacrifice if the convention were absolutely adhered to. I have not a clear recollection of what the Minister of Agriculture, upon the advice of his officers, thought necessary, but I do know the matter has engaged his attention. The proposal of my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) would require a great deal of consideration, because questions may arise with regard to patents as well as copyright- though the infringement would probably be more distinct in the case of literary works than with regard to patents-as to whether there had been wilful infringement.	As far as the remedy is
concerned, I do know that the one to which the Minister of Justice has alluded has been brought to bear in other provinces, because when I was practising at the Bar I had occasion to invoke with very good results that remedy which I understand to be available under the law of Quebec, and which if made use of by those authors might be found to afford a better remedy than that which they have succeeded in obtaining in the past. As my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) has brought this matter fully to the attention of the House. I shall now move to adjourn the debate, with the assurance to my hon. friend that his observations will receive the careful attention of the Minister of Agriculture.	-

Motion agreed to, and debate adjourned.
On motion of Sir Robert Borden, the House adjourned at 11.35 p.m.
Tuesday, February 16, 1915.
